title: Army advisory defense and relief at Duc Lap
location: Duc Lap and Dak Sak camp, Quang Duc Province
branches: Civilian Irregular Defense Group forces identified in the source
summary: American and Australian advisers, local defenders and reinforcing South Vietnamese troops resisted attacks at Duc Lap and Dak Sak. American helicopter reinforcement and evacuation attempts, together with Army artillery, supported the relief effort.

sources.title: U.S. Army official history — Erik B. Villard, Combat Operations: Staying the Course, October 1967 to September 1968, PDF page 685
U.S. Army official history — Erik B. Villard, Combat Operations: Staying the Course, October 1967 to September 1968, PDF page 686
Erik B. Villard, U.S. Army Center of Military History — Combat Operations: Staying the Course, October 1967 to September 1968 (2017) — printed pp. 660, 661, 662 (PDF pp. 687, 688, 689)

researchNotes: The district compound, nearby camp and relief forces are identified within a combined battle; this is not evidence that every surrounding Vietnamese action involved American infantry.

The complete account identifies U.S. Special Forces Detachment A–239 at Dak Sak, American advisers in the defense and counterattack, and executed American helicopter reinforcement and evacuation attempts. It names Battery A, 4th Battalion, 42d Artillery, and two 2d Battalion, 35th Infantry, platoons in the proposed Task Force Lance, then explicitly describes the battery deploying south of the camp. It does not separately narrate each infantry platoon’s arrival or combat. Allied irregular and South Vietnamese forces carried out the ground counterattacks, including American advisers with the irregulars.
The history says the crisis was over by 27 August, but does not assign a separate exact closing day to every American relief component. The existing month-precision end date is retained.

title: Thanh Duc plantation convoy ambush and relief
location: Highway 22 at Thanh Duc (Little Rubber) Plantation
summary: American convoy drivers and military police returned fire during an ambush at Thanh Duc. Infantry and armored cavalry counterattacked to relieve the trapped vehicles, and troops reentered the plantation the following morning.

sources.title: U.S. Army official history — Erik B. Villard, Combat Operations: Staying the Course, October 1967 to September 1968, PDF page 691
Erik B. Villard, U.S. Army Center of Military History — Combat Operations: Staying the Course, October 1967 to September 1968 (2017) — printed pp. 662, 663, 665 (PDF pp. 689, 690, 692)

researchNotes: Initial named-action inventory from the linked institutional narrative. Approximate dates and unit boundaries remain for deeper research.

The convoy belonged to the 6th and 7th Transportation Battalions. The relief included the 4th Battalion, 23d Infantry; Troop B, 3d Squadron, 4th Cavalry; and Company C, 3d Battalion, 22d Infantry. The fight, Sergeant William W. Seay’s action, the relief and the attempted vehicle recovery are one connected engagement.

The exact end date marks the explicitly dated 26 August reentry, when the history says the enemy had left during the night. It does not imply continuous fighting through that morning or a separate engagement for the search.
A different convoy from the 48th Transportation Group was ambushed farther north on 12 September. It is separately identified by date, convoy and position; it is not another account of this ambush.
aliases: Little Rubber Plantation convoy ambush, 25 August 1968
William W. Seay’s Thanh Duc action

summary: The 1st Battalion, 26th Marines landed and searched for Viet Cong and North Vietnamese forces.

sources.title: Gabrielle M. Neufeld — A Chronology of the U.S. Marine Corps, 1965–1969

Charles R. Smith, U.S. Marines in Vietnam: High Mobility and Standdown, 1969 (History and Museums Division, HQUSMC, 1988), original government edition retained via Internet Archive; printed pp. 309, 310 (PDF 325, 326)

researchNotes: First identification from inspected official historical or primary material. More detailed reports, local accounts and competing interpretations remain for later research.

The earlier Neufeld chronology, printed page 35 (original scan PDF 44), dates this BLT 1/26 Barrier Island landing/search September 15. Smith, printed pages 309–310 (original PDF 325–326), calls the operation Defiant Stand and explicitly places the first American landing September 7, the Korean landing September 12 and the contingents’ merger September 18. The same battalion, island and search mission support retaining one identity. Month precision preserves the differing official-history opening dates; September 18 bounds the documented final linkup phase, not every possible later shore duty.

Defiant Stand’s actual American landing, scattered firefights and allied blocking/sea-screening roles are described in the new source. Korean forces’ subsequent combat and most reported allied losses inflicted are not relabeled American infantry action. The prior reference and note remain available for comparison.

researchNotes: August 3 is the signing date, not a battle date. The settlement followed military defeat and required substantial land cessions; Article II provided for Indigenous hostages pending prisoner returns.

title: Jay Treaty enters into force after exchange of ratifications

researchNotes: Signed November 19, 1794; ratifications exchanged and entry into force October 28, 1795; proclaimed in the United States February 29, 1796. The proclamation is retained here as a later stage rather than counted as a second full treaty milestone.
Legal entry into force did not itself evacuate British posts. The executed 1796 handovers are indexed separately.

title: Treaty of Colerain signed with Muscogee representatives

researchNotes: Signed June 29, 1796; the ratification instrument is dated March 18, 1797. Signing is not treated as ratification or proof that an authorized post was built.

The printed ratification condition limits how the post provisions affect Georgia claims, soil and jurisdiction. The text does not establish an unlimited permanent land transfer or consent by every Muscogee community.

title: Navy corpsman and Marine Raiders treat casualties after a drone attack
location: Coalition base, northern Iraq; reported near Erbil
summary: A Navy corpsman serving with 2nd Marine Raider Battalion and accompanying Marines provided emergency care and helped evacuate French soldiers wounded in a drone strike.

sources.title: Defense Health Agency — October 6, 2026 account of Hernandez’s March 12 battlefield medical care
Task & Purpose — Navy corpsman’s account and official responses, October 30, 2026
French Ministry of the Armed Forces — March 13 notice of the March 12 Mala Qara attack

researchNotes: March 12 is the action date, rather than the October award reporting date. The DHA account confirms the date and medical response; Task & Purpose interviews the corpsman and identifies the French casualties. Marine officials withheld the exact country in their response, while the reporting links the incident to the French contingent near Erbil. The French ministry independently dates a drone attack at Mala Qara that wounded seven French soldiers, one fatally. This location association remains qualified rather than treated as a separately released U.S. operational coordinate.

This entry identifies U.S. casualty care after hostile action; it does not assert that the medical team exchanged fire or independently establish who launched the drone. Award descriptions of the mission use Epic Fury while Marine officials described the deployment as supporting Inherent Resolve. The action is kept under the latter continuing campaign without inferring an additional attack.

researchNotes: The July 15 execution report confirms the blockade resumed at 4 p.m. Eastern Time on July 14; this is not based solely on the July 13 announcement of intended action. It is a distinct phase from the existing April 13–June 18 record. The inspected October 10 report confirms continued enforcement but does not establish an end date. Aggregate diversion or boarding totals are not split into invented individual engagements.

The operation applies to traffic linked to Iranian ports, rather than every transit through the Strait of Hormuz. Recording a coercive operation does not resolve the disputed legal basis or imply that every stopped merchant vessel or crew was a combatant.

title: Attempted attacks on U.S. warships and strikes on three Iranian tankers

It reported disabling Downy near Kharg Island and Stark 1 near Jask, and destroying the unladen Kylo in the Gulf of Oman after directing its crew to abandon ship. The coordinated exchange is grouped here rather than counting each tanker as an independent whole battle.

The command’s claims of IRGC ownership, tanker use and military effect remain attributed. Iranian officials condemned the attacks on commercial vessels. Merchant crews are not automatically labeled combatants, and the entry does not resolve the legal justification.

summary: The Military Air Transport Service was activated as an Air Force major command, combining Air Transport Command and Naval Air Transport Service resources for military airlift. It became a principal organization for strategic transport before its later redesignation as Military Airlift Command.

sources.title: U.S. Air Mobility Command — Lineage and Honors History, PDF p. 1
U.S. Air Mobility Command — 100 Years of Mobility Airlift

researchNotes: The official lineage specifies June 1, 1948 for the activation. Later lineage consolidations in 1982 and 2016 are separate administrative actions and are not the date of this organization’s creation.

title: Bicol Peninsula USAFFE delaying actions
location: Ragay–Aloneros–Sumulong–Timbuyo approaches, Bicol Peninsula, Luzon, Philippines
branches: Philippine Army formations in U.S. service
summary: Detachments of USAFFE’s 51st Division (PA) used demolitions and infantry outposts to delay the Japanese advance from Legaspi. The 51st Engineer Battalion destroyed a bridge near Ragay during a December 17 patrol contact, and Company B, 52d Infantry, resisted near Timbuyo on December 22. General Albert Jones ordered the Bicol detachments to withdraw on December 23 as the Lamon Bay landing threatened their route back.

sources.title: Louis Morton, The Fall of the Philippines (U.S. Army CMH, 1993 reprint), chapter VI, printed pp. 109–112 (PDF pp. 128–131)
U.S. Army official history — The Fall of the Philippines, chapter 6 (HyperWar transcription)

researchNotes: This is one bounded operation by Philippine Army units under USAFFE, not a U.S. regular-infantry battle or a record of the unopposed December 12 Legaspi landing. It combines connected engineer and infantry delaying contacts instead of multiplying small encounters.

The start date is the first ground contact identified by Morton; the end date is Jones’s withdrawal order, not a claim that every detached company returned that day. His narrative describes a Filipino repulse at Timbuyo, while footnote 56 notes that the Japanese claimed victory. No numerical losses or force estimates are adopted.
Distinct from the South Luzon fighting-withdrawal record, which begins with the Lamon Bay assault and Jones’s wider withdrawal on December 24.

inventoryProvenance.method: Bounded component operation identified after comparison against all 13,240 serialized baseline records

title: Binalonan delaying defense
location: Binalonan and the withdrawal toward Tayug, Pangasinan, Luzon, Philippines
summary: The 26th Cavalry (Philippine Scouts) resisted Japanese tanks and infantry north and west of Binalonan on December 24. After repulsing the first attacks and counterattacking, the regiment held until General Wainwright ordered a delaying withdrawal. The Scouts began retiring in midafternoon and reached Tayug across the Agno by dusk.

sources.title: Louis Morton, The Fall of the Philippines (U.S. Army CMH, 1993 reprint), chapter VIII, printed pp. 137–138 (PDF pp. 156–157)
U.S. Army official history — The Fall of the Philippines, chapter 8 (HyperWar transcription)

researchNotes: This is the December 24 inland delaying action, a component of the Lingayen Gulf ground-defense umbrella. It is distinct from the December 22 Damortis fight and December 22–23 Rosario withdrawal; it is not another whole Lingayen landing.

The engaged regiment was the U.S. Army’s Philippine Scout cavalry. Morton records no Philippine Army infantry alongside it at Binalonan when Wainwright arrived. His approximate surviving-strength figure and general casualty claims are not adopted as verified loss totals.

title: Piis tank attack
location: Piis on the Mauban–Lucban road, Tayabas Province, Luzon, Philippines
summary: The 2d Platoon, Company C, 194th Tank Battalion, attached to the 1st Infantry (PA), attacked Japanese troops at Piis on December 26. Advancing along a narrow road, the American tanks met a prepared roadblock with antitank guns, field guns and machine guns. The attack failed; surviving tankers eventually made their way back to USAFFE lines.

sources.title: Louis Morton, The Fall of the Philippines (U.S. Army CMH, 1993 reprint), chapter XI, printed pp. 193–194 (PDF pp. 212–213)
U.S. Army official history — The Fall of the Philippines, chapter 11 (HyperWar transcription)

researchNotes: The attack was ordered by Major Ralph Rumbold of the 1st Infantry (PA) after General Jones attached the platoon to that regiment. This record covers the actual U.S. tank attack, not every Philippine Army contact during the Mauban withdrawal.

Jones’s preceding half-track patrol fight occurred on December 25 and is background to the roadblock, not a second action assigned to December 26. The infantry and recalled Scouts’ later stand at the Route 23 junction remains within the South Luzon umbrella.

The original government PDF says surviving tankers escaped; the cached HyperWar transcription says surviving tanks. The public account follows the original and does not claim the platoon’s remaining vehicles escaped. No numerical vehicle or personnel losses are adopted.

title: Moron counterattack by Philippine infantry and Scout cavalry
location: Moron and Batalan River, western Bataan, Luzon, Philippines
branches: Philippine Army formations in U.S. service
summary: Under Wainwright’s direction, the 1st Infantry (Philippine Army) and composite Troop E-F, 26th Cavalry (Philippine Scouts), counterattacked the Japanese 122d Infantry near Moron and drove it back to the Batalan River. The Scout cavalry then withdrew after suffering losses.

sources.title: Louis Morton — The Fall of the Philippines, chapter XVI, pp. 265–295 (U.S. Army official history; HyperWar transcription)
Louis Morton — The Fall of the Philippines (U.S. Army CMH, 1993 reprint of 1953 history), original printed pages

researchNotes: This is the 16 January counterattack north of the Mauban defensive line, a component of the existing Mauban line battle, not another whole-line battle. The Japanese entered Moron on 17 January after renewed attacks.

The U.S. Army Philippine Scouts in the 26th Cavalry were distinct from the Philippine Army 1st Infantry. No numerical loss total or claim about a last mounted cavalry charge is inferred from this source.

The original printed page 280 (PDF page 299) identifies the 26th Cavalry in the Troop G relief sentence. The HyperWar transcription’s 25th Cavalry there is an error; its counterattack paragraph correctly names the 26th.

title: Bani tank rearguard action
location: Back Road near Bani, eastern Bataan, Luzon, Philippines
summary: The U.S. 194th Tank Battalion and self-propelled 75-mm guns covered II Corps’ move to the Orion–Bagac line near Bani. They held off the Japanese 141st Infantry for several hours, then withdrew under artillery and mortar fire, leaving two disabled tanks when recovery proved impossible.

sources.title: Louis Morton — The Fall of the Philippines, chapter XVI, pp. 265–295 (U.S. Army official history; HyperWar transcription)
Louis Morton — The Fall of the Philippines (U.S. Army CMH, 1993 reprint of 1953 history), original printed pages

aliases: 194th Tank Battalion rearguard on the Back Road
researchNotes: Morton places the action on the morning of 26 January, with the enemy attack arriving between 0930 and 1030 and the tank column forced back around noon. This is a bounded rearguard contact during the broader Bataan withdrawal.

The source identifies the American tank battalion and self-propelled mounts but does not identify the exact firing unit operating each 75-mm gun here. No separate unit designation, personnel casualty count or Japanese loss claim is inferred.
This eastern Back Road action is geographically and operationally distinct from the West Road block behind the Mauban line and from the 25 January covering fire for the U.S. 31st Infantry.

title: Davao landing defense and withdrawal
location: Davao and surrounding heights, Mindanao, Philippines
branches: Philippine Army — Davao sector, including 2d Battalion, 101st Infantry
summary: Philippine Army troops under Lt. Col. Roger B. Hilsman defended the Davao sector when Japanese forces landed before dawn on 20 December. A machine-gun squad opposed the northern landing until a Japanese shell knocked it out. Hilsman withdrew the main force toward the surrounding hills, and Japanese troops occupied the city and airfield that afternoon.

sources.title: Louis Morton, U.S. Army — The Fall of the Philippines (1953; CMH 1993 reprint), original, printed 112–114, PDF p. 131

researchNotes: Morton, original printed pp. 112–114, identifies about 2,000 Philippine Army troops under Hilsman and limits direct landing opposition to one machine-gun squad. American participation is command of the USAFFE sector; no American rifle or machine-gun crew is inferred.

This is the December ground landing and withdrawal, distinct from the December 8 naval-air attack on William B. Preston and from B-17 raids on Davao shipping. It precedes, and does not subdivide, the existing April–May Mindanao defense umbrella.
The source reports Japanese casualties from the squad’s fire without a secure total. No numerical loss claim is adopted.

title: Zamboanga landing defense
branches: U.S. Army / USAFFE command — Zamboanga Sector
USAFFE Zamboanga Sector troops (unit composition unresolved)
summary: Troops of Lt. Col. Albert T. Wilson’s Zamboanga Sector briefly fought a Japanese naval landing force on 2 March before the Japanese occupied the town and established a seaplane base. General Sharp ordered Wilson on 6 March to withdraw into the mountains and conduct guerrilla operations.

sources.title: Louis Morton, U.S. Army — The Fall of the Philippines (1953; CMH 1993 reprint), original, printed 508, note 22, PDF p. 527

researchNotes: The full operative note in Morton, original printed p. 508 note 22, gives March 2, a brief fight with Wilson’s sector troops, and the March 6 withdrawal order. It cites Wilson’s Defense of Zamboanga and a translated Japanese landing account; those underlying reports have not been independently obtained.

American participation is Wilson’s command within the USAFFE Mindanao defense. Morton describes the southern force generally as predominantly Philippine Army, but does not identify the defender battalions or an American firing detachment at this contact; specific unit and nationality breakdowns remain unresolved.
The event ends with the March 2 contact. The March 6 order is aftermath, not evidence of continuous battle for four days; subsequent guerrilla activity is outside this entry.

title: Fort Frank pipeline-repair party fights near Calumpan
location: Near Calumpan, Cavite shore, Manila Bay, Philippines
branches: Filipino volunteers from Fort Frank (unit not specified)
summary: Fifteen American and Filipino volunteers from Fort Frank went ashore to repair its water pipeline, which the Japanese had cut near Calumpan. A Japanese patrol attacked before the repair was complete. Supported by 75-mm guns from the fort, the party repelled the patrol and returned safely without restoring the line.

sources.title: Louis Morton, U.S. Army — The Fall of the Philippines (1953; CMH 1993 reprint), original, printed 485–486, PDF p. 504

researchNotes: Morton, original printed pp. 485–486, dates the Japanese severing of the pipeline to February 16 and the repair-party engagement to February 19. The line was not repaired until March 9; the patrol’s unsuccessful repair mission is not represented as a successful restoration.
The narrative calls the party Americans and Filipinos but does not identify its unit breakdown. The Filipino volunteers are not automatically designated Philippine Scouts, civilians, or guerrillas.

Morton accepted the patrol’s claim to have destroyed the whole Japanese patrol, noting the absence of contrary evidence. That is not independent confirmation, so this entry uses only the supported repulse and safe-return outcome.

title: Swordfish evacuates President Quezon
location: Corregidor to San Jose, Panay, Philippines
summary: The U.S. submarine Swordfish evacuated Philippine President Manuel Quezon and his party to San Jose on Panay. The mission moved the president away from the besieged Manila Bay area before his later departure for Australia.

sources.title: Commander Task Force 51, U.S. Navy — Submarine Relief Activities, Philippine Area, May 15, 1942 (original report reproduction), report p. 1
Louis Morton, U.S. Army — The Fall of the Philippines (1953; 1993 government reprint), printed pp.399, 400

researchNotes: The May 15 Navy report records Swordfish’s arrival at Corregidor on February 19 and landing of Quezon’s party at San Jose on February 22. Month precision is retained for the evacuation phase rather than assuming the pickup day. The following Sayre evacuation was a separate leg and is not implied to have carried Quezon to Australia.

title: Sargo carries ammunition to Mindanao
summary: The U.S. submarine Sargo delivered small-arms ammunition to Polloc Harbor, Mindanao, and evacuated Army air-force ground personnel. The voyage formed part of the effort to supply American and Filipino forces cut off by the Japanese blockade.

sources.title: Commander Task Force 51, U.S. Navy — Submarine Relief Activities, Philippine Area, May 15, 1942 (original report reproduction), report p. 2
Robert J. Cressman, Naval Historical Center — Official Chronology of the U.S. Navy in World War II, 1942 (government text reproduced by HyperWar)
Louis Morton, U.S. Army — The Fall of the Philippines (1953; 1993 government reprint), printed p.399

researchNotes: The Navy chronology dates the delivery February 14; the contemporary May 15 relief report places the overall voyage in February 5–22 and identifies the Polloc Harbor destination and Army personnel evacuated. This is the delivery and connected evacuation episode, not 18 days of combat.

title: Seadragon delivers part of a relief cargo to Corregidor
summary: Seadragon carried food and fuel from Cebu to Corregidor and transferred part of its cargo to the naval vessel Pigeon. It took aboard radio-intelligence personnel and equipment, then waited off the entrance for possible further unloading before being ordered away.

sources.title: Commander Task Force 51, U.S. Navy — Submarine Relief Activities, Philippine Area, May 15, 1942 (original report reproduction), report p. 2
Robert J. Cressman, Naval Historical Center — Official Chronology of the U.S. Navy in World War II, 1942 (government text reproduced by HyperWar)
Louis Morton, U.S. Army — The Fall of the Philippines (1953; 1993 government reprint), printed p.399

researchNotes: The original May 15 Navy report dates the arrival April 8 and cancellation of further unloading April 10; these operative dates take precedence over Morton’s summary grouping the trip under March. The report distinguishes cargo loaded at Cebu from the smaller amount delivered at Corregidor. No claim is made that the whole load reached the garrison.

title: Snapper delivers food and evacuates personnel at Corregidor
summary: Snapper carried relief supplies from Cebu to Corregidor and transferred some food to Pigeon. The submarine also embarked naval personnel for evacuation; the transfer ended before all the food aboard had been unloaded.

sources.title: Commander Task Force 51, U.S. Navy — Submarine Relief Activities, Philippine Area, May 15, 1942 (original report reproduction), report p. 2
Commander Task Force 51, U.S. Navy — Submarine Relief Activities, Philippine Area, May 15, 1942 (original report reproduction), report p. 3
Robert J. Cressman, Naval Historical Center — Official Chronology of the U.S. Navy in World War II, 1942 (government text reproduced by HyperWar)
Louis Morton, U.S. Army — The Fall of the Philippines (1953; 1993 government reprint), printed p.399

researchNotes: The May 15 Navy report and Navy chronology date the Corregidor visit April 9; Morton’s summary groups it with March missions and describes the loaded food and fuel as if fully unloaded. The original report instead says Pigeon left after a partial food transfer, and Snapper later discharged remaining food at Fremantle. This record uses the documented visit and avoids treating the whole cargo as delivered.

title: Spearfish evacuates personnel from Corregidor
summary: The U.S. submarine Spearfish took personnel, including nurses, out of the Corregidor area shortly before the garrison surrendered.

sources.title: Commander Task Force 51, U.S. Navy — Submarine Relief Activities, Philippine Area, May 15, 1942 (original report reproduction), report p. 3
Robert J. Cressman, Naval Historical Center — Official Chronology of the U.S. Navy in World War II, 1942 (government text reproduced by HyperWar)
Louis Morton, U.S. Army — The Fall of the Philippines (1953; 1993 government reprint), printed p.399

researchNotes: The May 15 Navy relief report and Navy chronology place this evacuation on May 3. The original report specifically identifies Army and Navy nurses among the passengers. A passenger total is omitted pending comparison with the submarine’s detailed records.

title: Navy and Army air evacuation of MacArthur’s party
summary: Navy PT boats carried General Douglas MacArthur, his family and members of his headquarters from Corregidor to Mindanao. Army B-17s then flew the party to Australia, completing the connected sea and air evacuation.

sources.title: Robert J. Cressman, Naval Historical Center — Official Chronology of the U.S. Navy in World War II, 1942 (government text reproduced by HyperWar)
Louis Morton, U.S. Army — The Fall of the Philippines (1953; 1993 government reprint), printed pp.359, 360

researchNotes: The Navy chronology explicitly dates the PT-boat departure March 11; Morton’s printed p.359 instead says March 12. The start follows the naval chronology, with that discrepancy retained. Morton’s printed p.360 supports the successful Army air leg and arrival in Australia March 17. The sea and air legs form one connected evacuation, not separate battles.

title: Royce bomber mission returns to the Philippines
location: Australia to Mindanao and targets in the Philippines
summary: A force of Army B-25 and B-17 bombers led by Brigadier General Ralph Royce flew from Australia to Mindanao and attacked Japanese shipping, airfields and harbor facilities in the Philippines. After two days of operations, the surviving bombers returned to Australia.

sources.title: National Museum of the U.S. Air Force — Royce Special Mission to Mindanao

researchNotes: The National Museum of the U.S. Air Force dates the outward flight April 11, 1942 and describes two days of bombing operations before return. The entry groups the connected mission and leaves the terminal date unspecified rather than deriving an exact return day. Claimed ship sinkings and an aircraft loss total are omitted pending comparison with unit records.

title: Seawolf supplies Corregidor and evacuates airmen
location: Darwin to Corregidor, with return to Surabaya
summary: Seawolf carried .50-caliber ammunition to Corregidor and took out Army and Navy airmen, torpedoes and submarine spare parts on its return voyage.

sources.title: Commander Task Force 51, U.S. Navy — Submarine Relief Activities, Philippine Area, May 15, 1942 (original report reproduction), report p. 1

researchNotes: The contemporary May 15 Navy report dates Seawolf’s Corregidor visit January 27–28 within an overall January 16–February 7 voyage. Month precision is retained for the local delivery and connected evacuation pending comparison with the submarine’s detailed log. The interval of the entire patrol is not labeled as continuous fighting.

title: Trout supplies Corregidor and removes valuables
summary: Trout delivered antiaircraft ammunition to Corregidor and removed gold, silver, securities and mail. The mission brought supplies through the blockade and carried valuables away from the threatened fortress.

sources.title: Robert J. Cressman, Naval Historical Center — Official Chronology of the U.S. Navy in World War II, 1942 (government text reproduced by HyperWar)
Commander Task Force 51, U.S. Navy — Submarine Relief Activities, Philippine Area, May 15, 1942 (original report reproduction), report p. 1

aliases: Trout Corregidor ammunition and gold mission
researchNotes: The Navy chronology dates the visit February 3; the May 15 relief report independently confirms the ammunition delivery and removal of valuables and passengers. Tonnage and monetary values are omitted rather than combining different retrospective totals. This is separate from Trout’s later combat patrol and its February 9 attack already indexed.

title: Japanese air attacks and ground defense at Hickam Field
summary: Japanese bombers and fighters struck the Army bomber base, aircraft, hangars and barracks. Army personnel returned machine-gun fire, while military personnel, Honolulu firefighters and civilian depot workers rescued casualties and fought fires.

sources.title: Arakaki and Kuborn — 7 December 1941: The Air Force Story (Pacific Air Forces Office of History, 1991) — Hickam, pp.66–69,81–110; civilian firefighting pp.106–108
Conn, Engelman and Fairchild — Guarding the United States and Its Outposts, chapter VII, The Attack and the Response, pp.187–194

researchNotes: A site-specific component of the same 7 December Oahu attack; its parent and sibling records overlap and must not be added as separate whole battles.
The 1941 Hawaiian Air Force was part of the U.S. Army Air Forces; the modern Air Force base name does not identify a separate U.S. Air Force service in 1941.
The original printed pp.106–108 document the Honolulu mutual-aid response and civilian Hawaiian Air Depot employees fighting fires. They were civilian responders, not enemy combatants.
Unarmed B-17s arriving from California encountered the attack and landed at Hickam and other Oahu fields; no separate event is created for each aircraft or casualty.

title: Japanese air attacks and fighter response at Wheeler Field
location: Wheeler Field and airspace over eastern Oahu, Hawaii Territory
summary: Japanese dive bombers and fighters attacked Wheeler’s parked pursuit aircraft, hangars and barracks. Ground crews moved and armed surviving aircraft, and P-36 fighters took off and engaged Japanese aircraft over the Kaneohe area.

sources.title: Arakaki and Kuborn — 7 December 1941: The Air Force Story (Pacific Air Forces Office of History, 1991) — Wheeler attacks pp.62–66 and fighter response pp.76–79
Conn, Engelman and Fairchild — Guarding the United States and Its Outposts, chapter VII, The Attack and the Response, pp.187–194

researchNotes: A site-specific component of the same 7 December Oahu attack; its parent and sibling records overlap and must not be added as separate whole battles.

This combines the strike on the fighter base with the sorties launched there, rather than creating individual pilot or aircraft entries. Fighters rearmed at Wheeler could also have launched earlier from Haleiwa.

Published accounts differ in precise timing, routes and aircraft-loss credits. The descriptive core adopts neither a minute-by-minute reconstruction nor an unqualified tally of enemy aircraft destroyed.

title: Japanese strafing and attempted fighter defense at Bellows Field
location: Bellows Field, Waimanalo, Oahu, Hawaii Territory
branches: U.S. Army: 298th Infantry, Hawaii National Guard
summary: Japanese fighters strafed Bellows, where Army personnel returned fire from the ground and pursuit pilots tried to take off. Two P-40s were shot down during departure; a B-17 arriving from California also crash-landed at the field.

sources.title: Arakaki and Kuborn — 7 December 1941: The Air Force Story (Pacific Air Forces Office of History, 1991) — Bellows pp.69,78,128–131
Conn, Engelman and Fairchild — Guarding the United States and Its Outposts, chapter VII, The Attack and the Response, pp.187–194

researchNotes: A site-specific component of the same 7 December Oahu attack; its parent and sibling records overlap and must not be added as separate whole battles.

The original printed p.128 identifies Hawaii National Guard personnel of the 298th Infantry positioning .30-caliber antiaircraft machine guns at the runway’s end; the Guard contribution is kept within the Army.
The two P-40 departure losses are described in the detailed official history; one pilot survived. No implication is made that every pilot or ground casualty had the same fate.
The B-17 landing is included within the local raid episode; this is not a second bombing raid or a separately counted ferry flight.

title: Army fighter sorties from Haleiwa during the Oahu attack
location: Haleiwa auxiliary field and airspace over Oahu, Hawaii Territory
summary: Army ground crews armed and launched P-40 and P-36 fighters from the outlying Haleiwa strip. The pilots engaged Japanese aircraft over Ewa and northern Oahu and used Haleiwa and Wheeler for repeated sorties.

sources.title: Arakaki and Kuborn — 7 December 1941: The Air Force Story (Pacific Air Forces Office of History, 1991) — Air Force Opposition, pp.76–80
Conn, Engelman and Fairchild — Guarding the United States and Its Outposts, chapter VII, The Attack and the Response, pp.187–194

researchNotes: A site-specific component of the same 7 December Oahu attack; its parent and sibling records overlap and must not be added as separate whole battles.

This identifies a distinct launch base and connected fighter-defense episode, not a claim that Haleiwa suffered a major Japanese strike. The 1991 PACAF account calls it un-attacked; the Army history describes an isolated strafing pass. That disagreement is not resolved here.
The official histories differ on initial takeoff timing and include uncertain individual victory claims. Exact times and an unqualified enemy-loss total are omitted.
The 47th Pursuit Squadron’s aircraft were at Haleiwa for gunnery training. The sorties and work of ground crews are grouped, without separate records for each pilot.

title: Japanese air attacks and defense of Naval Air Station Kaneohe Bay
location: Naval Air Station Kaneohe Bay, Oahu, Hawaii Territory
summary: Japanese fighters and bombers attacked patrol aircraft on the water and ramp and struck a hangar at Kaneohe. Naval personnel and Marine guards returned fire, while crews tried to save aircraft from burning areas.

sources.title: Commander Patrol Wing One, K. McGinnis — Report of Japanese Air Attack on Kaneohe Bay, 1 January 1942 (complete report transcription)
Cressman and Wenger — Infamous Day: Marines at Pearl Harbor (USMC, 1992), p.4: Kaneohe Marine detachment

aliases: Kaneohe Bay Naval Air Station attack, 7 December 1941
researchNotes: A site-specific component of the same 7 December Oahu attack; its parent and sibling records overlap and must not be added as separate whole battles.

Kaneohe was a Navy air station in December 1941. The Marine detachment’s armed response is documented on printed p.4 of the official USMC history; modern Marine Corps ownership is not used to infer the 1941 service roles.

Patrol Wing One’s contemporary report was read in full as a HyperWar transcription. NHHC access attempts failed, so a scan of the signed original was not inspected. The report’s estimated attack timings, counts and victory claims are not adopted as an exact reconstruction.
Aircraft absent on dawn patrol were not on the station when it was struck. The Ward-associated dawn-patrol submarine action remains in its existing separate naval record.

title: Japanese air attacks and ground defense at Ewa Mooring Mast Field
location: Ewa Mooring Mast Field, Oahu, Hawaii Territory
summary: Japanese fighters and dive bombers repeatedly strafed Marine Aircraft Group 21’s field and parked aircraft. Marines fired from the ground and fought fires, while Navy medical personnel aided casualties and Marine crews later serviced Enterprise aircraft that landed there.

sources.title: Cressman and Wenger — Infamous Day: Marines at Pearl Harbor (USMC, 1992), part1, p.14: opening Ewa attack
Cressman and Wenger — Infamous Day: Marines at Pearl Harbor (USMC, 1992), part2, pp.16–23: Ewa defense, medical and aircraft support

researchNotes: A site-specific component of the same 7 December Oahu attack; its parent and sibling records overlap and must not be added as separate whole battles.

The complete Ewa section, They Caught Us Flat-Footed, printed pp.14–23, was read. It describes rifle and aircraft-machine-gun resistance, firefighting, medical response and later rearming/refueling of Navy Enterprise SBDs as one connected field episode.
Navy participation rests on the USN medical officer and corpsman on printed p.18 and the Enterprise aircraft on pp.22–23, rather than a generic multi-service label.
The account also describes family members seeking safety, including a child present at the field. Civilians and dependents in danger are not characterized as combatants.
Ground-fire victory claims, exact Japanese losses and claims that every local aircraft was permanently destroyed are omitted.

title: Initial Japanese air raid on Wake
location: Wake and Peale Islands, Wake Atoll
summary: Japanese land-based bombers struck the airfield and Pan American facilities; Marine antiaircraft crews returned fire as the airborne patrol missed the raid.

sources.title: R. D. Heinl, Jr., The Defense of Wake (HQ USMC, 1947), printed pp. 13–16; original PDF pp. 20–23
Robert J. Cressman, A Magnificent Fight: Marines in the Battle for Wake Island (HQ USMC, 1992), printed pp. 1–5; original part 1, PDF pp. 3–7
Robert J. Cressman, A Magnificent Fight: Marines in the Battle for Wake Island (HQ USMC, 1992), printed pp. 6–7; original part 2, PDF pp. 1–2

researchNotes: Dates are Wake local civil dates, west of the International Date Line; they are not the same calendar dates then observed in Hawaii. No present-day UTC offset is back-applied.
Component of the existing whole defense of Wake; directory rows overlap and must not be added as distinct battles.
Includes the first raid across the airstrip, Camp 2 and Peale, rather than separate records for each bombed installation. Pan American Chamorro employees and other civilians suffered casualties.
The Philippine Clipper departed after the raid with passengers and some Pan American employees; this is contextual evacuation, not an executed armed search or reinforcement flight.

title: Marine air attack on a submarine southwest of Wake
summary: A VMF-211 patrol fighter bombed and strafed a surfaced submarine believed Japanese; its identity and the damage remained uncertain.

sources.title: R. D. Heinl, Jr., The Defense of Wake (HQ USMC, 1947), printed pp. 30; original PDF pp. 38
Robert J. Cressman, A Magnificent Fight: Marines in the Battle for Wake Island (HQ USMC, 1992), printed pp. 14–15; original part 2, PDF pp. 9–10
Robert J. Cressman, Official Chronology of the U.S. Navy in World War II, 1941, December 11 entry

researchNotes: Dates are Wake local civil dates, west of the International Date Line; they are not the same calendar dates then observed in Hawaii. No present-day UTC offset is back-applied.

Heinl (1947), Tyson and Cressman’s detailed 1992 narrative place Kliewer’s attack on December 12; the 1999 Navy chronology places an apparently corresponding tentative RO 66 attack on December 11. December 12 follows the detailed narratives, with the contrary date retained here.
The contact is an actual attack, not a confirmed sinking. The oil slick and submergence do not establish the target’s loss, and RO 66 is not treated as a secure identification.
This single contact is distinct from Triton’s torpedo salvo. It was mentioned in older notes but had no separate baseline event; no duplicate December 11 version is added.

title: December 15 flying-boat raid on Wake
location: Wake and Peale Islands, Wake Atoll
summary: Japanese flying boats bombed and strafed the atoll near dusk, including the Peale batteries; the attack killed a civilian.

sources.title: R. D. Heinl, Jr., The Defense of Wake (HQ USMC, 1947), printed pp. 32; original PDF pp. 40
Robert J. Cressman, A Magnificent Fight: Marines in the Battle for Wake Island (HQ USMC, 1992), printed pp. 16–17; original part 2, PDF pp. 11–12

researchNotes: Dates are Wake local civil dates, west of the International Date Line; they are not the same calendar dates then observed in Hawaii. No present-day UTC offset is back-applied.
Component of the existing whole defense of Wake; directory rows overlap and must not be added as distinct battles.
The detailed accounts agree on an actual dusk attack, although aircraft numbers and precise bomb impact areas differ. No aircraft destruction or installation-damage tally is adopted.

title: December 16 air raids on Wake
location: Wake and Peale Islands, Wake Atoll
summary: Marine patrol fighters warned the antiaircraft batteries of approaching land-based bombers; a later flying boat bombed and strafed Peale.

sources.title: R. D. Heinl, Jr., The Defense of Wake (HQ USMC, 1947), printed pp. 32; original PDF pp. 40
Robert J. Cressman, A Magnificent Fight: Marines in the Battle for Wake Island (HQ USMC, 1992), printed pp. 17; original part 2, PDF pp. 12

researchNotes: Dates are Wake local civil dates, west of the International Date Line; they are not the same calendar dates then observed in Hawaii. No present-day UTC offset is back-applied.
Component of the existing whole defense of Wake; directory rows overlap and must not be added as distinct battles.
Heinl identifies the daylight attack and the later flying-boat raid. Cressman’s 1992 account confirms the daylight fighter warning and air defense but gives a different bomber strength and time.
Claims of Japanese aircraft shot down or damaged conflict with the Japanese account summarized in 1992; no numerical loss claim is adopted.

title: Wake relief expedition deployment and recall
location: Pearl Harbor–central Pacific east of Wake Atoll
summary: A force carrying Marine reinforcements, fighters and supplies sailed toward Wake under Saratoga’s cover, but was recalled before reaching the atoll.

sources.title: R. D. Heinl, Jr., The Defense of Wake (HQ USMC, 1947), printed pp. 37–39; original PDF pp. 45–48
Robert J. Cressman, A Magnificent Fight: Marines in the Battle for Wake Island (HQ USMC, 1992), printed pp. 16–19; original part 2, PDF pp. 11–14

researchNotes: Dates are Wake local civil dates, west of the International Date Line; they are not the same calendar dates then observed in Hawaii. No present-day UTC offset is back-applied.

The dates are normalized to the Wake-side calendar: Tangier, Neches and escorts sailed at 1730 Hawaii time December 15, explicitly 1400 December 16 on Wake in Cressman. Saratoga followed the next Hawaii day. Recall on Hawaii December 22 was Wake December 23.

This records an executed naval deployment through recall, not a completed landing, successful resupply or battle fought by Task Force 14 at Wake. Planned civilian and wounded evacuation aboard Tangier never occurred.
The operation included fuel and supply movements at sea. The projected Jaluit diversion and proposed final independent Tangier dash were not executed attacks and do not receive battle records.
The two histories differ in their retrospective judgments of the recall; those counterfactual assessments are not adopted.

title: PBY liaison and evacuation flight to Wake
summary: A Navy PBY reached Wake with mail and relief instructions, then departed for Midway carrying official reports and Major Bayler.

sources.title: R. D. Heinl, Jr., The Defense of Wake (HQ USMC, 1947), printed pp. 34; original PDF pp. 42
Robert J. Cressman, A Magnificent Fight: Marines in the Battle for Wake Island (HQ USMC, 1992), printed pp. 19; original part 2, PDF pp. 14
Robert J. Cressman, A Magnificent Fight: Marines in the Battle for Wake Island (HQ USMC, 1992), printed pp. 20; original part 3, PDF pp. 1

researchNotes: Dates are Wake local civil dates, west of the International Date Line; they are not the same calendar dates then observed in Hawaii. No present-day UTC offset is back-applied.
The interval covers the completed arrival and next-morning departure on Wake civil dates. It does not date the later arrival at Pearl Harbor.
The flight actually completed liaison and a limited evacuation. It did not deliver Task Force 14’s proposed Marine reinforcement, radar or fighter squadron.
Bayler was the departing passenger; the individual is not given a separate personal-action row.

title: Wilkes landing defense and counterattack
summary: Wilkes defenders contained a Japanese landing, counterattacked the occupied battery position, and later obeyed the atoll surrender order.

sources.title: R. D. Heinl, Jr., The Defense of Wake (HQ USMC, 1947), printed pp. 52–59; original PDF pp. 62–73
Robert J. Cressman, A Magnificent Fight: Marines in the Battle for Wake Island (HQ USMC, 1992), printed pp. 24–35; original part 3, PDF pp. 5–16

researchNotes: Dates are Wake local civil dates, west of the International Date Line; they are not the same calendar dates then observed in Hawaii. No present-day UTC offset is back-applied.
A geographically distinct action within the final December 23 assault, under its existing parent; it is not a second capture of the whole atoll.
The initial beach defense, night containment and dawn counterattack form one connected episode. Platt’s and McAlister’s converging groups are not split into personal attacks.
Despite the defeat of the landing party on Wilkes, broken communications delayed knowledge of the general surrender. Air attacks and a final advance continued before the surrender party arrived.
No exact enemy annihilation or casualty tally is adopted.

Heinl, printed p. 53 (original PDF p. 65), identifies the provisional Battery F defenders as Marine searchlight personnel, sailors and civilians trained for antiboat fire and infantry defense; Navy participation is therefore explicit.

title: Insular Force Guard defense of Agana’s Plaza de España
location: Plaza de España and San Antonio district, Agana (Hagåtña), Guam
summary: The Guam Insular Force Guard used rifles and machine guns to halt briefly Japanese naval troops advancing from Dungcas Beach into Agana. A few Marines also fought at the Plaza de España. Firing stopped before Governor George J. McMillin signed the island’s surrender.

sources.title: Captain George J. McMillin — 11 September 1945 report and surrender letter, reprinted by the National Park Service from Guam Recorder (1972)
Hough, Ludwig and Shaw — Pearl Harbor to Guadalcanal (official Marine Corps history, 1958), Part II, chapter 2, printed pp. 75–78 (PDF pp. 84–87)
National Park Service — Guam in World War II, Imperial Japanese Invasion (excerpts from Cyril J. O’Brien’s official Marine Corps commemorative history)

researchNotes: This is the December 10 Guam local ground fight, corresponding to December 9 in Hawaii. It is a tactical component of the December 8–10 defense, not a second whole invasion or a separate surrender event.

The Guard was a Guamanian infantry force in U.S. government service, distinct from the volunteer naval militia and Insular Patrol police. The Marine official history names First Lieutenant Charles S. Todd as commander; the NPS account also identifies a few Marines in the Plaza fighting. Navy participation here includes the governor and station command and negotiations; no naval rifle party is inferred.

McMillin’s 1945 report says the Guard briefly checked the advance, firing stopped about 0545 after a car-horn signal, and negotiations and written surrender followed. He wrote from memory after his wartime notes were destroyed; approximate times are not treated as independently synchronized evidence.

The principal Marine barracks force was in the rifle-range position near Sumay and received orders not to resist after surrender. Its presence elsewhere on the island does not justify assigning the full Marine garrison to the Plaza firefight. No force-strength, casualty or enemy-loss total is asserted.

title: Nevada’s fighting sortie and beaching
location: Battleship Row and the harbor channel, Pearl Harbor, Oahu, Hawaii
summary: Nevada’s crew returned antiaircraft fire after the battleship was torpedoed. The ship got underway from Battleship Row, came under further air attack while moving down the channel, and was beached inside the harbor.

sources.title: USS Nevada commanding officer — Report of December 7, 1941 Raid, December 15, 1941 (primary report reproduced by HyperWar)
Robert J. Cressman, Naval Historical Center — Official Chronology of the U.S. Navy in World War II, 1941 (HyperWar reproduction)

researchNotes: This is the battleship’s connected defense, movement and beaching within the Pearl Harbor attack, not an additional whole raid. The contemporary report’s aircraft-destruction claims and preliminary bomb-hit estimates are not adopted as verified totals.
Nevada’s report describes the decision to leave the vicinity of the burning Arizona. No claim is made that the ship completed a sortie to sea.

title: Helm fires on a submarine off Pearl Harbor
location: Tripod Reef near the Pearl Harbor entrance, Oahu, Hawaii
summary: While clearing Pearl Harbor during the air attack, Helm sighted a submarine near the entrance and opened fire after it surfaced again off Tripod Reef. The destroyer reported no observed hits, and the submarine submerged.

sources.title: C. E. Carroll, USS Helm — Action during air raid on December 7, report of December 11, 1941 (primary report reproduced by HyperWar)

aliases: USS Helm Tripod Reef submarine contact
researchNotes: Helm’s report places the initial sighting at 0817 and gunfire at about 0820, local time. It records no observed hit; the possible fragment-hit language later in the report is not promoted to a confirmed sinking.

The report also describes air defense and near-miss bomb damage during the connected sortie. This row identifies the discrete submarine gunfire contact and does not assign an unproven midget-submarine number or crew identity.

title: Gamble mistakenly fires on Thresher off Oahu
summary: The light minelayer Gamble mistakenly fired on the American submarine Thresher off Oahu. Thresher had expected to rendezvous with Litchfield and mistook the similarly shaped converted destroyer for that ship.

sources.title: Robert J. Cressman, Naval Historical Center — Official Chronology of the U.S. Navy in World War II, 1941 (HyperWar reproduction)

aliases: USS Gamble USS Thresher mistaken-identity firing
researchNotes: The official Navy chronology identifies this as friendly fire, not an attack on a confirmed Japanese submarine. No combat damage or casualty tally from Gamble’s gunfire is asserted.
A sailor aboard Thresher had been injured by heavy seas before this encounter and died before the submarine reached port the next day; his original injury is not attributed to Gamble’s fire.

title: Enterprise scout-bombers encounter the Pearl Harbor attack
location: Oahu air approaches and Ford Island, Hawaii
summary: SBD scout-bombers from Enterprise approached Oahu while the Japanese attack was in progress. Some were lost to Japanese aircraft and American fire; surviving aircraft landed and joined searches for the Japanese carriers.

sources.title: Robert J. Cressman, Naval Historical Center — Official Chronology of the U.S. Navy in World War II, 1941 (HyperWar reproduction)

aliases: Enterprise SBD arrivals during Pearl Harbor raid
researchNotes: This record covers the morning scout-bomber flight encountering the attack and its connected response. Enterprise itself remained at sea; the flight is not described as a Japanese attack on the carrier.

This is distinct from the evening friendly-fire incident involving Enterprise F4F fighters attempting to land at Ford Island. Aircraft and personnel loss totals are not adopted from a single summary account.

title: Friendly fire on Enterprise fighters returning to Oahu
location: Ford Island approaches and the Pearl Harbor–Hickam area, Oahu, Hawaii
summary: American antiaircraft fire hit Navy F4F fighters from Enterprise as they approached Oahu after dark. The fighters had been directed to land at Ford Island; aircraft were lost and pilots killed in the mistaken engagement.

sources.title: Robert J. Cressman, Naval Historical Center — Official Chronology of the U.S. Navy in World War II, 1941 (HyperWar reproduction)
Leatrice R. Arakaki and John R. Kuborn, Pacific Air Forces Office of History — 7 December 1941: The Air Force Story (1991), printed p. 140, PDF p. 154

aliases: Ford Island returning Wildcat friendly fire
researchNotes: The Navy chronology and the original Air Force history describe American fire on returning Navy fighters, not a second Japanese night raid. The numerical aircraft-loss tally is omitted; different accounts classify shot-down aircraft, crash landings and fuel-exhaustion losses differently.

The original Air Force history describes armed personnel on Oahu and returning Navy airmen. This record does not assign each aircraft loss to an individual gun crew or service. The morning SBD arrivals were a separate flight.

title: Yorktown strikes at Jaluit, Makin and Mili
location: Jaluit and Mili, Marshall Islands; Makin, Gilbert Islands
summary: Yorktown aircraft attacked shipping and shore structures at Jaluit, Makin and Mili despite severe weather. Carrier fighters defended the group while escort destroyers searched for downed aircrews.

sources.title: Office of Naval Intelligence — Early Raids in the Pacific Ocean (1943), Yorktown air-group action, printed pp.27–33; original PDF pp.47–53
Robert J. Cressman — Official Chronology of the U.S. Navy in World War II, 1942

aliases: Yorktown component of the Marshall–Gilbert raids, 1 February 1942
researchNotes: A distinct carrier group and set of objectives within the preserved February 1 Marshall–Gilbert operation; the umbrella and its Enterprise component remain separate overlapping records, not additional whole raids.

The original account follows the Jaluit, Makin and Mili sorties as one connected carrier episode. Bad weather scattered the Jaluit group, complicated recovery and led to cancellation of a projected second attack; that canceled attack is not listed as executed.
Mili offered few identifiable targets; some structures were only presumed to be storehouses or a water tank. Target identification and precise damage are not treated as certain.

The escort search and defense against a reconnaissance flying boat are included in the same carrier-group action. Neither an unsuccessful search nor every lost aircraft is split into a separate engagement.
The date is the local raid date given by the official sources; no present-day UTC offset is back-applied.

title: Defense of Lexington during the canceled Rabaul raid
location: Waters northeast of Rabaul, off Bougainville, South Pacific
summary: Lexington fighters, scout bombers and ships’ antiaircraft guns engaged Japanese patrol aircraft and two bomber attacks while the carrier maneuvered to avoid bombs. The planned attack on Rabaul was abandoned.

sources.title: Office of Naval Intelligence — Early Raids in the Pacific Ocean (1943), Action off Rabaul, printed pp.35–40; original PDF pp.62–67
Robert J. Cressman — Official Chronology of the U.S. Navy in World War II, 1942

aliases: Lexington air battle off Bougainville, 20 February 1942
researchNotes: The actual February 20 defensive air combat is distinguished from the planned February 21 strike and conditional surface bombardment of Rabaul. Neither planned attack was carried out.

The official narrative documents radar-directed combat air patrols, attacks on reconnaissance flying boats, successive bomber formations and antiaircraft fire from the carrier group. O’Hare’s interception remains part of the combined defense rather than a separate personal-action record.
Army heavy bombers appeared in the proposed Rabaul plan; that planning reference does not establish Army participation in this naval defensive action.

The wartime account explicitly records disagreement between fighter pilots and shipboard observers about antiaircraft results. Enemy aircraft-loss totals and individual victory credits are not asserted as independently confirmed.

Four American fighters were damaged by friendly antiaircraft fire according to the 1943 account; this is retained as a source observation within the same confused air battle, not an additional enemy attack.
The date is the local action date given by the official sources; no present-day UTC offset is back-applied.

title: Yorktown patrol interception during the Coral Sea rendezvous
location: Coral Sea near the carrier-force rendezvous
summary: Yorktown fighters investigated a radar contact and engaged a Japanese flying boat as the American carrier groups joined in the Coral Sea.

sources.title: Office of Naval Intelligence, The Battle of the Coral Sea (1943), official NHHC 2017 republication, printed pp. 8 (PDF pp. 24)

researchNotes: Dates follow the local operational calendar used in the Coral Sea reports, west of the International Date Line; they are not substituted with the previous Hawaii/U.S. calendar day. Exact clock minutes and modern UTC offsets are not imposed on the source timelines.

The narrative identifies an actual fighter contact during the morning rendezvous, distinct from the May 2 submarine attack, Tulagi bombing, and later May 7 patrol engagements. Its aircraft-destruction credit is not used as a verified loss tally.
A submarine sighting mentioned in the same passage did not produce a located target on the follow-up search; no separate attack is inferred from it.
A bounded air-defense component under the preserved Coral Sea parent, not a separate whole battle or a record for an individual pilot.

title: May 7 carrier patrol interceptions in the Coral Sea
summary: Carrier fighters intercepted a reconnaissance flying boat and later Japanese aircraft approaching the force; recovery continued after dark amid poor visibility and aircraft-identification confusion.

sources.title: Office of Naval Intelligence, The Battle of the Coral Sea (1943), official NHHC 2017 republication, printed pp. 14–15 (PDF pp. 30–31)
USS Yorktown, Serial 063, 16 May 1942: air operations of 7 May; original report pp. 5–7 (same PDF pages), National Archives scan via HyperWar

researchNotes: Dates follow the local operational calendar used in the Coral Sea reports, west of the International Date Line; they are not substituted with the previous Hawaii/U.S. calendar day. Exact clock minutes and modern UTC offsets are not imposed on the source timelines.
The official narrative groups the daytime and evening contacts under combat air patrol on May 7. This record follows that documented patrol phase; it is distinct from the outbound attack on Shoho.

The original Yorktown report records radar-directed patrol action and an evening encounter before enemy aircraft appeared near the carriers during recovery. Aircraft-type labels and destruction claims varied and are not standardized into verified totals.

The report and narrative include a ship-time zone change on May 7 and conflicting exact minutes for the twilight appearances. Only the shared local date is adopted; a precise synchronized minute is not asserted.

The proximity of Japanese planes does not establish that their intended strike successfully delivered bombs or torpedoes on the American carriers that evening. Proposed night surface action was not executed and receives no battle record.

title: Lexington’s shipboard defense, evacuation and scuttling
location: Coral Sea, southeast of the Louisiade Islands
summary: Lexington maneuvered and fired on the Japanese aircraft attacking the carrier. Damage-control parties initially contained fires and flooding, but later internal explosions and spreading fires disabled the ship. Destroyers and cruisers rescued her crew; after abandonment Phelps sank the carrier with torpedoes.

sources.title: U.S. Navy Office of Naval Intelligence — The Battle of the Coral Sea (1943; official NHHC 2017 reprint), Attack on Lexington and Sinking of Lexington, 2017 printed pp. 28–37 (PDF pp. 44–53)

aliases: USS Lexington damage control and abandonment, May 8, 1942
researchNotes: This is the connected shipboard defense, damage control, evacuation and scuttling component of the May 8 carrier battle. The outgoing carrier strikes and fighter interceptions are covered by the existing May 8 air-battle record; this is not another whole battle.

Morris passed firefighting hoses and took personnel off; Anderson and Hammann also rescued survivors, while Phelps, Dewey and cruiser boats recovered men from the water. The phases are grouped rather than counted as separate rescue or individual award events.

The wartime narrative links the fatal later explosions to accumulated gasoline vapor, while acknowledging the initial cause was uncertain aboard ship. No exact hit, torpedo, crew-rescue percentage, casualty or enemy-aircraft tally is adopted.

inventoryProvenance.method: Complete official operative shipboard narrative read and compared against all 13,276 serialized baseline records.

title: Yorktown’s shipboard defense and firefighting
location: Coral Sea, southeast of the Louisiade Islands
summary: Yorktown maneuvered to avoid torpedoes and returned antiaircraft fire during the Japanese carrier attack. A bomb penetrated below the flight deck and started fires. Repair and fire parties, including the mortally wounded Lieutenant Milton E. Ricketts, fought the fires, and the damaged carrier remained underway.

sources.title: U.S. Navy Office of Naval Intelligence — The Battle of the Coral Sea (1943; official NHHC 2017 reprint), Attack on Yorktown and Results of a Direct Hit, 2017 printed pp. 23–24 and 48 (PDF pp. 39–40 and 64)

aliases: USS Yorktown bomb damage and repair parties, May 8, 1942
researchNotes: This record covers the ship’s defensive maneuvering, gunfire and damage control during the May 8 attack. Its aircraft’s outgoing strikes and combat patrols remain in the existing air-battle component. The June 1942 torpedoing and sinking of Yorktown at Midway are separate operations.
Ricketts’s action is included as part of the fire parties’ response, not a separate personal-heroism or Medal of Honor event. No precise casualty or enemy aircraft-loss total is adopted.

The source reports bomb damage and torpedo avoidance at Coral Sea; the ship is not described as sunk or torpedoed in this action. Repair work at Pearl Harbor later in May is outside this day’s record.

inventoryProvenance.method: Complete official operative shipboard and direct-hit sections read and compared against all 13,276 serialized baseline records.

title: Henley rescues survivors and scuttles Neosho
location: Coral Sea, at the drifting Neosho
summary: Henley reached the disabled Neosho and took off the surviving men aboard, including Sims survivors who had reached the oiler. After Neosho’s captain requested that the unsalvageable ship be sunk, Henley used torpedoes and gunfire to scuttle her. The destroyer then searched for missing men.

sources.title: U.S. Navy Office of Naval Intelligence — The Battle of the Coral Sea (1943; official NHHC 2017 reprint), Loss of the Neosho and Sims, 2017 printed p. 45 (PDF p. 61)
USS Neosho — May 25, 1942 report on the May 7 attack, loss and search for survivors, PDF pp. 5–6 (original National Archives document reproduced by HyperWar)
Robert J. Cressman — Official Chronology of the U.S. Navy in World War II, May 1942 (HyperWar reproduction)

aliases: USS Henley rescue of Neosho and Sims survivors
researchNotes: This is an executed post-battle rescue and scuttling episode following the May 7 attack. It is attached to the Coral Sea operation as a consequence even though the main battle umbrella ends May 8; the parent’s fighting dates are not extended to imply continued carrier combat.
The damaged oiler remained afloat between the attack and rescue. May 7 damage and May 11 American scuttling are not conflated into a second Japanese attack or an additional independently sunk ship.

Phillips’s original May 25 report and the Navy narrative both date the sinking May 11. Exact sinking minutes and survivor or weapon counts are not adopted. The later Helm raft recovery remains a separate actual search contact with its exact day unresolved.

inventoryProvenance.method: Compiled official narrative and original commander-report operative page compared with the complete serialized baseline.

title: Helm recovers Neosho raft survivors
location: Coral Sea, Neosho survivor search area
summary: During the search following Neosho’s loss, Helm recovered surviving men from a drifting life raft. They had abandoned the damaged oiler during the May 7 attack. The survivors were gravely weakened by exposure, and one died after being brought aboard.

sources.title: U.S. Navy Office of Naval Intelligence — The Battle of the Coral Sea (1943; official NHHC 2017 reprint), Loss of the Neosho and Sims, 2017 printed p. 45 (PDF p. 61)
USS Neosho — May 25, 1942 report on the May 7 attack, loss and search for survivors, PDF pp. 5–6 (original National Archives document reproduced by HyperWar)
Robert J. Cressman — Official Chronology of the U.S. Navy in World War II, May 1942 (HyperWar reproduction)

aliases: USS Helm rescue of Neosho raft survivors
researchNotes: The month is known, but the exact day is unresolved. Phillips’s May 25 original Neosho report gives May 16; the ONI narrative, officially reprinted in 2017, gives May 17; Cressman’s Navy chronology places the same Helm recovery on May 21. No day is silently preferred, and these are not three separate rescues.

Phillips said he had not received Helm’s detailed search report. All three accounts identify Helm and the same small party of Neosho raft survivors; the disagreement concerns date rather than whether the American rescue occurred. Helm’s own log or search report remains to locate.

Dated only to May 1942; no continuous combat or rescue activity from May 16 through May 21 is implied. This is a post-battle recovery consequence under the preserved Coral Sea parent, distinct from Henley’s removal of survivors still aboard Neosho.

inventoryProvenance.method: Actual rescue identified across three complete operative accounts; month precision retained because exact dates conflict. Full 13,276-record comparison found no independent equivalent.

title: Midway PBY reconnaissance of the Japanese approach
location: Waters west and northwest of Midway Atoll
summary: Navy PBY patrols located the Japanese occupation force on June 3 and reported the approaching air strike and carrier force early on June 4. Reconnaissance crews transmitted contact reports despite antiaircraft fire and attacks by Japanese aircraft.

sources.title: Logan C. Ramsey, U.S. Navy — Air Operations of Midway Defense Forces, report dated 15 June 1942 (complete identified reproduction), paragraphs 11–12
Office of Naval Intelligence — Battle of Midway (1943; official NHHC 2017 republication), printed pp. 9–10, 13–14 (PDF pp. 27–28, 31–32)

researchNotes: The June 3 sightings concerned occupation-force shipping, initially reported as the main body; the Japanese carrier force was located on June 4. These are distinct contacts within the same island-based reconnaissance effort.
The search, enemy encounters and contact reports were an island-based reconnaissance effort, distinct from the separate night torpedo attack, Army bombing and carrier strikes.
The reports use Midway operational dates and zone-plus-12 time. They differ on the exact minutes of some contacts, and each aircraft’s sighting forms part of the same reconnaissance effort.

title: Midway-based VT-8 Avengers attack the Japanese carrier force
summary: The Midway-based TBF detachment of Torpedo Squadron 8 attacked the Japanese carrier force under heavy fighter and antiaircraft opposition. A badly damaged Avenger returned to Eastern Island.

sources.title: Logan C. Ramsey, U.S. Navy — Air Operations of Midway Defense Forces, report dated 15 June 1942 (complete identified reproduction), paragraphs 11–12
Office of Naval Intelligence — Battle of Midway (1943; official NHHC 2017 republication), printed pp. 17–18 (PDF pp. 35–36)
Robert J. Cressman — Official Chronology of the U.S. Navy in World War II, June 4, 1942

researchNotes: These TBF Avengers flew from Midway, separately from Hornet’s embarked VT-8 TBD Devastators. The Army B-26 torpedo bombers approaching the same Japanese force were a different service component.
The surviving pilot could not establish the attack’s results while evading fighters. Wartime torpedo-hit reports and enemy-aircraft claims are not adopted as confirmed damage.
The executed June 4 attack and return were distinct from the detachment’s earlier transit and the separate carrier-launched torpedo attacks.

title: Midway Marine strikes against the Japanese carrier force
summary: VMSB-241 launched separate SBD-2 and SB2U-3 groups from Eastern Island. The SBDs attacked a carrier, while the SB2Us, under fighter pressure, attacked nearby battleships; surviving aircraft returned through continued opposition.

sources.title: M. A. Tyler, USMC — Report of Activities of VMSB-241 during June 4 and June 5, 1942, dated 12 June 1942 (complete identified reproduction)
Hough, Ludwig and Shaw — Pearl Harbor to Guadalcanal (official Marine Corps history, 1958), Part V chapter 4, printed pp. 221–225 (full identified reproduction)
Office of Naval Intelligence — Battle of Midway (1943; official NHHC 2017 republication), printed pp. 18–19 (PDF pp. 36–37)

researchNotes: Both groups used glide-bombing approaches. The SBDs’ carrier recognition was uncertain, and the SB2Us turned to battleships when fighter opposition prevented a further search for the carriers.

The wartime squadron report claimed bomb hits. The later official Marine history states that the attacks scored no hits; the claims are not treated as confirmed damage or as evidence that these aircraft sank a carrier.

An evening follow-up sortie failed to find the reported burning carrier, and its leader did not return. That unsuccessful search remains context of the day’s connected sorties, rather than another completed attack.
The outbound bombing missions were separate from VMF-221’s fighter defense over Midway and from the Army and Navy torpedo attacks.

title: Marine shore batteries answer a submarine bombardment at Midway
location: Midway Atoll, Sand and Eastern Islands
summary: The Japanese submarine I-168 shelled Midway before dawn on June 5. Marine searchlights illuminated the submarine and shore batteries returned fire before it submerged.

sources.title: H. D. Shannon, USMC — 6th Defense Battalion report of action on June 4 and night of June 4–5, dated 13 June 1942 (complete identified reproduction)
R. D. Heinl, Jr., USMC — Marines at Midway (1948), original edition, printed pp. 40 (PDF pp. 49)
Office of Naval Intelligence — Battle of Midway (1943; official NHHC 2017 republication), printed pp. 38–39 (PDF pp. 56–57)

researchNotes: The submarine was observed late on June 4, but the recorded shelling and return fire occurred after midnight on June 5. This is separate from the June 4 carrier air raid and the submarine’s June 6 attack on Yorktown and Hammann.

The 6th Defense Battalion report identifies Baker Battery’s 5-inch fire, Dog and Easy Batteries’ 3-inch fire, Cast Battery’s star shells and searchlight illumination. These are Marine shore units; no American naval gunfire is inferred.

The defenders reported hits on the submarine, but those reports do not establish damage. The battalion reported no damage or casualties from this bombardment; the submarine submerged and was not sunk.

title: Midway Marine strike on the retiring Japanese cruisers
summary: VMSB-241 SBDs and SB2Us followed an oil trail to the damaged cruisers Mogami and Mikuma and their escorts. The Marines attacked under antiaircraft fire and returned to Midway after losing one bomber.

sources.title: M. A. Tyler, USMC — Report of Activities of VMSB-241 during June 4 and June 5, 1942, dated 12 June 1942 (complete identified reproduction)
R. D. Heinl, Jr., USMC — Marines at Midway (1948), original edition, printed pp. 40–41 (PDF pp. 49–50)
Office of Naval Intelligence — Battle of Midway (1943; official NHHC 2017 republication), printed pp. 39 (PDF pp. 57)

aliases: Marine attack on Mogami and Mikuma
researchNotes: The initial orders and wartime squadron report called the targets battleships. The later Marine narrative identifies the damaged ships as Mogami and Mikuma, which had collided while retiring.

The SBD group made a dive-bombing attack and the SB2Us a glide-bombing attack. The report describes a burning Marine aircraft continuing its attack, but no deliberate collision with a cruiser is asserted.
Reported bomb hits, exact damage credit and enemy-loss claims are not adopted. This June 5 island-based sortie is separate from the June 6 attacks by aircraft from Enterprise and Hornet.

title: Carrier fighter patrols defend the Midway task forces
location: U.S. carrier task forces near Midway Atoll
summary: Carrier fighters intercepted Japanese dive bombers and torpedo planes approaching Yorktown in successive raids. Enterprise continued fighter protection and its patrols also engaged Japanese seaplanes shadowing the task forces.

sources.title: Office of Naval Intelligence — The Battle of Midway (1943), official NHHC 2017 republication, printed pp. 26–29 (PDF pp. 44–47)
Captain G. D. Murray — USS Enterprise action report, Serial 0133, June 8, 1942, reporting June 4–6 (complete HyperWar transcription)
Rear Admiral R. A. Spruance — Task Force Sixteen action report, Serial 0144-A, June 16, 1942, reporting June 4–6 (complete HyperWar transcription)

aliases: June 4 carrier combat air patrols at Midway
researchNotes: Dates follow the U.S. operational calendar in the Midway reports. Enterprise and Spruance use zone plus ten; the ONI narrative uses Midway time, zone plus twelve, two hours behind. Exact clock times are not treated as identical across these accounts.

The airborne patrol and interception phase includes the two approaches to Yorktown and Enterprise patrol contacts with shadowing seaplanes. It does not adopt aircraft-destruction credits as a verified loss tally.
Yorktown fighters refueled and rearmed aboard Enterprise before intercepting the later raid; aircraft operating from another carrier are not treated as a new service or an additional battle.
This connected air-defense phase accompanies the outbound carrier strikes. Yorktown’s shipboard gunfire, damage control, abandonment and subsequent salvage are related phases.

title: Carrier pursuit strike northwest of Midway
location: Northwest of Midway Atoll across the International Date Line
summary: Enterprise and Hornet launched long-range strikes in pursuit of a reported damaged Japanese carrier force. The bombers did not locate that objective, but attacked small Japanese warships before returning to the carriers after dark.

sources.title: Office of Naval Intelligence — The Battle of Midway (1943), official NHHC 2017 republication, printed pp. 35–38 (PDF pp. 53–56)
Captain G. D. Murray — USS Enterprise action report, Serial 0133, June 8, 1942, reporting June 4–6 (complete HyperWar transcription)
Rear Admiral R. A. Spruance — Task Force Sixteen action report, Serial 0144-A, June 16, 1942, reporting June 4–6 (complete HyperWar transcription)

aliases: June 5 Enterprise and Hornet pursuit strike
Midway carrier search and small-warship attacks, June 5
researchNotes: Dates follow the U.S. operational calendar in the Midway reports. Enterprise and Spruance use zone plus ten; the ONI narrative uses Midway time, zone plus twelve, two hours behind. Exact clock times are not treated as identical across these accounts.
The intended carrier target was not found. The episode consists of the executed search, bombing contacts with small warships and night recovery, rather than an attack on an unlocated carrier.

Enterprise describes a light cruiser and undetermined damage. Spruance describes two small vessels, doubts hits, and considers them destroyers; the ONI narrative records no observed direct hits. A named ship, exact target count and confirmed damage are not assigned.
The two carrier groups form one connected pursuit strike, not separate records for each aircraft group or bombing pass. Downed-aircrew recovery is a related rescue phase.

title: Army B-17 attack on the Midway occupation force
location: Pacific Ocean west of Midway Atoll
summary: Army B-17s flying from Midway bombed the Japanese transport force approaching the atoll after Navy patrol aircraft reported it. The bombers reported hits, but the extent of damage remained uncertain.
