Craven and Cate, editors — The Army Air Forces in World War II, Vol. I, pp. 457–458 (PDF pp. 522–523)
Carter and Mueller — USAAF Combat Chronology, June 3, 1942, Seventh AF (PDF p. 21)

aliases: Sweeney B-17 attack on the Midway transport force
researchNotes: The target was part of the Japanese occupation force, although early contact reports called it the main body. This was the afternoon Army bombing mission of June 3; the Navy flying-boat torpedo attack followed during the night of June 3–4.
The postwar Army Air Forces history sharply reduced the original damage claims and described only probable minor damage to a transport. No claimed warship hit or sinking is treated as established.

title: Army B-17 pursuit attacks west of Midway
location: Pacific Ocean west and northwest of Midway Atoll
summary: Army B-17s from Midway bombed retiring Japanese cruisers in the morning and searched farther northwest for reported carriers during the afternoon. Clouds prevented the later flights from finding those carriers, but they attacked cruiser contacts before returning.

sources.title: Office of Naval Intelligence — The Battle of Midway, June 3–6, 1942 (official 2017 reprint), pp. 39–40 (PDF pp. 57–58)
Carter and Mueller — USAAF Combat Chronology, June 5, 1942, Seventh AF (PDF p. 22)
Craven and Cate, editors — The Army Air Forces in World War II, Vol. I, pp. 459–461 (PDF pp. 524–526)

aliases: Midway B-17 Flights 92 and 93 pursuit missions
researchNotes: The morning B-17 attack followed a separate Marine bombing attack on the retiring cruiser force. The afternoon Army flights sought reported carriers but made cruiser contacts instead.
Contemporary reports claimed bomb hits, but those claims do not establish the ships damaged or the extent of damage. No Japanese cruiser sinking is attributed to these Army attacks.
The Army chronology calls the June 5 cruiser attack its last strike of the battle; its June 6 entry separately records continued search and a mistaken attack on a U.S. submarine.

title: Army B-17s mistakenly bomb an American submarine near Midway
location: Pacific Ocean west of Midway Atoll
summary: Army B-17s searching from Midway for Japanese ships bombed an American submarine after mistaking it for an enemy surface vessel. The submarine submerged and suffered no damage.

sources.title: Carter and Mueller — USAAF Combat Chronology, June 6, 1942, Seventh AF (PDF p. 23)
Office of Naval Intelligence — The Battle of Midway, June 3–6, 1942 (official 2017 reprint), p. 44 (PDF p. 62)
Robert J. Cressman — Official Chronology of the U.S. Navy in World War II, June 7, 1942 (HyperWar reproduction)

researchNotes: The Army chronology dates the mistaken attack to June 6 and leaves the submarine unnamed. The wartime Navy combat narrative also places it on June 6 and identifies the boat as Grayling, which crash-dived when bombs fell nearby.

The later Navy chronology records an undamaged Grouper being bombed by Army B-17s on June 7. Whether this was a separate contact or a conflicting date and identification has not been established; it is not counted here as a second incident.
Reports that the target disappeared after the bombs fell were mistaken impressions of a sinking. No American submarine loss or damage is attributed to this attack.

title: Nautilus torpedo attacks and evasion at Midway
summary: Nautilus attempted torpedo attacks on Japanese warships near Midway, including a damaged carrier, and endured repeated depth-charge counterattacks.

sources.title: Office of Naval Intelligence — The Battle of Midway (1943), official NHHC 2017 republication, Nautilus action, printed p.25 / PDF p.43
Robert J. Cressman — Official Chronology of the U.S. Navy in World War II, June 1942

aliases: Nautilus at the Battle of Midway
researchNotes: This groups the submarine’s connected June 4 combat rather than counting each torpedo, depth charge or target approach as another battle.

The wartime ONI account identifies the damaged carrier as Soryu and credits a final sinking blow; Cressman’s later chronology identifies Kaga and describes torpedoes failing to explode. The shared attack and counterattack are retained, while a confirmed carrier sinking, exact target identity and torpedo-hit total are not asserted here.
The complete relevant ONI page and Cressman June 4 entry were read. The original submarine patrol report was not inspected; comparison with that report and Japanese records remains necessary.

title: Yorktown’s shipboard defense and evacuation at Midway
summary: Yorktown and her escorts fired on Japanese aircraft while the carrier maneuvered against bombing and torpedo attacks. Crewmen fought fires, repaired the flight deck and restored propulsion after the first attack. Later torpedo damage disabled the ship, and destroyers rescued the evacuating crew.

sources.title: Office of Naval Intelligence — The Battle of Midway (1943), official NHHC 2017 republication, Yorktown air attacks and shipboard response, printed pp.26–30 / PDF pp.44–48
U.S.S. Yorktown — Loss in Action, June 4–7, 1942, original scanned damage report, sections I–II, printed pp.1–2 / PDF pp.4–5

researchNotes: A shipboard defense, damage-control and evacuation component under the whole Midway operation. Outgoing carrier strikes and airborne fighter patrols have their own connected entries; this is not a second whole carrier battle.

The first dive-bomber attack and later torpedo-plane attack on June 4 are retained as one connected ship-defense episode. The later salvage operation and June 6 submarine attack are separately dated phases.

The damage report was compiled from surviving officers’ recollections and explicitly notes missing technical details. The combat narrative and damage report give different clock times; only their shared date is used. No exact hit, casualty, rescue or aircraft-victory tally is adopted.
The account describes evacuation after loss of power and heavy listing. Yorktown remained afloat; neither abandonment nor the June 4 air attacks are described here as the date of her final sinking.

title: Yorktown towing and salvage after abandonment
summary: Hughes guarded Yorktown and recovered men after the carrier’s abandonment. Vireo took the carrier in tow, and salvage parties worked with support from Hammann and other destroyers to extinguish fires and reduce the list. A submarine attack interrupted the work on June 6; Yorktown capsized and sank the next morning.

sources.title: Office of Naval Intelligence — The Battle of Midway (1943), official NHHC 2017 republication, End of the Yorktown, printed pp.49–53 / PDF pp.67–71
U.S.S. Yorktown — Loss in Action, June 4–7, 1942, original scanned damage report, June5–7 narrative and salvage, printed pp.3,8–9 / PDF pp.6,11–12
Robert J. Cressman — Official Chronology of the U.S. Navy in World War II, June 1942

researchNotes: The date span covers executed guarding, rescue, towing and salvage plus the ship’s eventual loss. It does not imply continuous combat or another Japanese attack on June 7.

Vireo actually towed the ship and Hammann supplied power, firefighting water and pump support. Navajo and Seminole were dispatched but did not arrive before Yorktown sank; their planned arrival is not recorded as completed salvage assistance.

The existing June 6 I-168 attack remains the specific submarine encounter. This connected salvage record explains the work interrupted by that attack and is not an additional carrier or destroyer loss.

The reports differ on exact tow, torpedo and sinking minutes and on technical damage explanations. These are not reconciled into a precise synchronized clock. No claimed salvage success or numerical casualty total is adopted.

title: Florida Island covering landings at Haleta and Halavo
location: Haleta and Halavo Peninsula, Florida Island (Nggela), Solomon Islands
summary: Marines of the 1st Battalion, 2d Marines, occupied positions near Haleta and Halavo to cover the Tulagi and Gavutu landings. No Japanese force was encountered ashore; Navy ships exchanged fire with shore guns while covering the Halavo approach.

sources.title: Hough, Ludwig and Shaw — Pearl Harbor to Guadalcanal (official USMC history, 1958), Part VI chapter 3, printed pp. 263–264 (original PDF pp. 267–268)
John L. Zimmerman, USMC — The Guadalcanal Campaign (1949), chapter II, printed pp. 26–27 (original PDF pp. 36–38)
Office of Naval Intelligence — The Landing in the Solomons (1943; official NHHC 2017 republication), printed pp. 34–42 (PDF pp. 52–60)

researchNotes: The Haleta force landed before the Tulagi assault, while the rest of the battalion covered the Gavutu approach from Halavo. The Florida beachheads were security positions; subsequent attacks on Tulagi and Gavutu met separate ground resistance.
The Halavo approach drew fire from Gavutu, and covering Navy vessels engaged guns on Gavutu and Bungana. The patrols on the Florida beachheads found no Japanese ground force.
RAAF officer C. E. Spencer guided the Haleta landing. His role was local guidance with the landing force, separate from the carrier aircraft supporting the operation.
Company B was later withdrawn from Florida and committed to the first Tanambogo landing attempt; that subsequent fighting took place on Tanambogo.

title: Tulagi landing and southeastern ridge fighting
location: Beach Blue, Hill 208 and Hill 281, Tulagi, Solomon Islands
summary: The 1st Raider Battalion landed at Beach Blue and advanced southeast with support from the 2d Battalion, 5th Marines, and Navy gunfire. After repelling night attacks, the Marines converged on the defended ravine near Hill 281 and broke organized resistance on August 8.

sources.title: Hough, Ludwig and Shaw — Pearl Harbor to Guadalcanal (official USMC history, 1958), Part VI chapter 3, printed pp. 263–267 (original PDF pp. 267–271)
John L. Zimmerman, USMC — The Guadalcanal Campaign (1949), chapter II, printed pp. 27–33 (original PDF pp. 38–44)
Office of Naval Intelligence — The Landing in the Solomons (1943; official NHHC 2017 republication), printed pp. 34–37, 55–56, 71–72 (PDF pp. 52–55, 73–74, 89–90)

aliases: Beach Blue landing and Tulagi ridge battle
researchNotes: The Beach Blue landing was unopposed. The main fighting developed as the raiders approached the southeastern ridges and cave positions; the quiet landing beach did not describe the later ground action.
Navy gunfire liaison parties worked with the raider headquarters. The supporting ships could bombard designated positions, but Marines still had to close with defended caves and ravines.
Organized resistance ended on August 8; patrols continued to find isolated defenders afterward. The later occupation and defense of the island are consequences of this assault.

title: Gavutu landing and Hill 148 fighting
location: Gavutu seaplane base and Hill 148, Solomon Islands
summary: The 1st Parachute Battalion landed by boat on Gavutu under fire from the island and Tanambogo. Marines fought inland around Hill 148, held their positions overnight, and were reinforced by the 3d Battalion, 2d Marines, on August 8.

sources.title: Hough, Ludwig and Shaw — Pearl Harbor to Guadalcanal (official USMC history, 1958), Part VI chapter 3, printed pp. 267–271 (original PDF pp. 271–275)
John L. Zimmerman, USMC — The Guadalcanal Campaign (1949), chapter II, printed pp. 33–40 (original PDF pp. 44–51)
Office of Naval Intelligence — The Landing in the Solomons (1943; official NHHC 2017 republication), printed pp. 42–44, 57–59, 72–73 (PDF pp. 60–62, 75–77, 90–91)
Carolyn A. Tyson — A Chronology of the United States Marine Corps, 1935–1946, August 7–9, 1942, printed pp. 25–27

researchNotes: The parachute battalion made a seaborne landing. The damaged seaplane ramp forced boats toward a pier exposed to fire, and positions on Tanambogo continued to enfilade the Gavutu beachhead.

Navy boats landed troops and evacuated wounded while supporting ships fired on island positions. Marine reinforcements on August 8 relieved the depleted assault force and helped reduce remaining positions.
The Marine histories also describe supporting aircraft striking friendly positions on Hill 148. No numerical casualty total is assigned to enemy or friendly fire.
The neighboring Tanambogo assaults were connected to securing Gavutu but occurred on a separate island and across the causeway.
The assault and reinforcement occupied August 7–8, while the Marine chronology places final securing of Gavutu with the island group on August 9. The interval includes the connected clearance phase.

title: Tanambogo assaults and causeway fighting
location: Tanambogo and the causeway from Gavutu, Solomon Islands
summary: A first Marine landing attempt on Tanambogo withdrew under heavy fire on August 7. Infantry and tanks renewed the assault on August 8 while another Marine force crossed the causeway from Gavutu; close fighting and clearance continued into August 9.

sources.title: Hough, Ludwig and Shaw — Pearl Harbor to Guadalcanal (official USMC history, 1958), Part VI chapter 3, printed pp. 268–270 (original PDF pp. 272–274)
John L. Zimmerman, USMC — The Guadalcanal Campaign (1949), chapter II, printed pp. 35–39 (original PDF pp. 46–50)
Office of Naval Intelligence — The Landing in the Solomons (1943; official NHHC 2017 republication), printed pp. 57–59, 72–75 (PDF pp. 75–77, 90–93)

aliases: 3/2 infantry and tank assault on Tanambogo
researchNotes: The first attempt used Company B, 1st Battalion, 2d Marines, after its Florida security mission. RAAF officer Spencer guided the approach; a fuel fire lit the landing area, and Japanese fire forced a withdrawal and evacuation.

The renewed assault used Company I and elements of Company K, 3d Battalion, 2d Marines, with tanks from the 2d Tank Battalion. Navy lighter crews landed troops and tanks under fire, and Buchanan provided close gunfire support.
The Navy narrative describes the principal positions held late on August 8. The Marine histories carry the remaining close fighting through August 9; the interval includes that connected clearance.
Accounts disagree on some tank-crew details, supporting-ship identities and exact timings. No enemy-loss count, guaranteed gunfire result or individual tank-kill total is asserted.

title: Amphibian-tractor resupply and casualty evacuation at Gavutu
location: Gavutu and the transport President Adams, Solomon Islands
summary: Marine amphibian tractors carried supplies and personnel from President Adams to Gavutu and returned with wounded during August 8–9. In one evacuation, a tractor crew used its machine guns to cover wounded Marines pinned down by a Japanese position.

sources.title: Hough, Ludwig and Shaw — Pearl Harbor to Guadalcanal (official USMC history, 1958), Part VI chapter 3, printed pp. 270 (original PDF pp. 274)
John L. Zimmerman, USMC — The Guadalcanal Campaign (1949), chapter II, printed pp. 38–39 (original PDF pp. 49–50)
Office of Naval Intelligence — The Landing in the Solomons (1943; official NHHC 2017 republication), printed pp. 72–75 (PDF pp. 90–93)

aliases: Gavutu amphibian-tractor supply and ambulance service
3d Platoon, Company A, 2d Amphibian Tractor Battalion
researchNotes: The documented service began around noon on August 8 and continued through the following night; the tractors were reembarked before sundown on August 9. Several supply and evacuation trips formed the same platoon operation.

The tractor crews were Marines. President Adams supported the ship-to-shore service, and the 1949 Marine history identifies American Red Cross representative D. S. Oman as supervising evacuation of the wounded. His civilian medical-support role is distinct from the armed tractor crews.

The account does not date the under-fire pickup more closely than this interval. It was an emergency rescue during the support mission, not proof that amphibian tractors were generally employed as assault tanks.

title: Southern screening force fights off Savo Island
location: South and southeast of Savo Island, Solomon Islands
summary: Chicago, Patterson and Bagley engaged Japanese warships alongside the Australian cruiser Canberra. Japanese gunfire disabled Canberra, a torpedo damaged Chicago, and Patterson continued fighting after being hit.

sources.title: Office of Naval Intelligence — The Battle of Savo Island (1943), official NHHC 2017 republication, southern-force action, printed pp.4,9–13 / PDF pp.22,27–31

U.S. Naval War College — The Battle of Savo Island, August 9th, 1942: Strategical and Tactical Analysis (1950), original scanned volume, Canberra damage and the inquiry disagreement, printed pp.128–129 / PDF pp.190–191

researchNotes: Dates follow the local operational calendar. These contacts occurred after midnight on August 9 within the night commonly called August 8–9; incompatible exact clock minutes in the reports are not treated as independent engagements.

A tactical component of the existing Savo battle, grouping the southern force rather than creating a separate battle for each ship damaged. HMAS Canberra was an Australian warship; HMAS Australia had carried Rear Admiral Crutchley to a conference and was absent from this particular contact.
Patterson transmitted a warning and fired guns; its torpedo order was not carried out. Bagley did launch torpedoes, but observed explosions do not independently establish hits or sinkings.

Canberra’s initial underwater damage remains disputed: the wartime ONI narrative describes torpedo hits, while the later Naval War College analysis cites an Australian inquiry finding them improbable. This record neither establishes Japanese torpedo hits on Canberra nor assigns them to Bagley.
Chicago’s torpedo damage belongs to this surface action. No new Japanese ship-loss total or confirmed sinking is inferred from American gun-flash and searchlight observations.

title: Northern screening force fights off Savo Island
location: Between Savo and Florida Islands, Solomon Islands
summary: Vincennes, Quincy and Astoria returned fire as Japanese cruisers attacked the northern screen; Helm and Wilson also took part. Quincy and Vincennes sank after the engagement, while the burning Astoria remained afloat into the morning.

sources.title: Office of Naval Intelligence — The Battle of Savo Island (1943), official NHHC 2017 republication, northern-group action, printed pp.13–26 / PDF pp.31–44

U.S. Naval War College — The Battle of Savo Island, August 9th, 1942: Strategical and Tactical Analysis (1950), original scanned volume, losses of Vincennes, Quincy and Astoria, printed pp.289–295 / PDF pp.359–365

researchNotes: Dates follow the local operational calendar. These contacts occurred after midnight on August 9 within the night commonly called August 8–9; incompatible exact clock minutes in the reports are not treated as independent engagements.

A tactical phase within the preserved whole battle, not three additional whole battles for the lost cruisers. Shellfire, fires and torpedo damage disabled the formation; Astoria’s subsequent loss is followed in the rescue and salvage component.

Astoria briefly ceased fire when its captain feared friendly ships were being engaged, then resumed. This mistaken identification is not evidence that its initial Japanese targets actually were American.

Wilson fired on enemy illumination; Helm’s intermittent fire and attempted approach were affected by uncertain identification. A planned destroyer attack is not represented as a completed coordinated torpedo strike.
The ONI account’s speculative submarine sightings, turret-hit claims and detailed minute-by-minute reconstruction are not adopted as confirmed submarine attacks or an exact enemy-damage tally.

title: Ralph Talbot fights the withdrawing Japanese force
location: North and northwest of Savo Island, Solomon Islands
summary: The picket destroyer Ralph Talbot exchanged gunfire and launched torpedoes at Japanese cruisers withdrawing from the Savo action. Badly damaged, the destroyer survived and its crew worked to keep it afloat.

sources.title: Office of Naval Intelligence — The Battle of Savo Island (1943), official NHHC 2017 republication, Ralph Talbot encounter, printed pp.26–27 / PDF pp.44–45

U.S. Naval War College — The Battle of Savo Island, August 9th, 1942: Strategical and Tactical Analysis (1950), original scanned volume, Ralph Talbot action and Japanese withdrawal, PDF pp.327–329,334–335
National Park Service — Down but Not Out: USS Ralph Talbot at Savo Island, At Savo Island and After the Battle

researchNotes: Dates follow the local operational calendar. These contacts occurred after midnight on August 9 within the night commonly called August 8–9; incompatible exact clock minutes in the reports are not treated as independent engagements.

A separate picket-ship contact after the attacks on the southern and northern cruiser groups, linked to the same Savo battle. Damage control immediately afterward is part of this contact’s aftermath, not another enemy engagement.

The initial belief that friendly destroyers were firing was an identification error. The postwar Naval War College reconstruction attributes the gunfire to Tenryu, Furutaka and Yubari; no American friendly-fire attack on Ralph Talbot is asserted.

Wartime ONI identified a supposed Tone-class cruiser and credited a searchlight hit; the later reconstruction identifies Yubari and explains its extinguished light as part of withdrawal. A confirmed searchlight-destruction claim or Japanese sinking is not repeated.

Sources disagree on exact times, torpedo details, casualty figures and the side of the destroyer’s list. The core gun-and-torpedo contact and survival are retained without imposing those contested totals.

title: Chicago and Patterson exchange mistaken gunfire
location: Near the disabled HMAS Canberra southeast of Savo Island, Solomon Islands
summary: Chicago and Patterson briefly exchanged gunfire in a mistaken-identification incident while Patterson was assisting Canberra. Both stopped firing after recognition; the accounts report no resulting damage or hits.

sources.title: Office of Naval Intelligence — The Battle of Savo Island (1943), official NHHC 2017 republication, mistaken Chicago–Patterson exchange, printed p.30 / PDF p.48

U.S. Naval War College — The Battle of Savo Island, August 9th, 1942: Strategical and Tactical Analysis (1950), original scanned volume, Chicago and Patterson accounts, printed pp.282,288–289 / PDF pp.352,358–359

researchNotes: Dates follow the local operational calendar. These contacts occurred after midnight on August 9 within the night commonly called August 8–9; incompatible exact clock minutes in the reports are not treated as independent engagements.
A genuine exchange of fire around 0525 local time, separate from the earlier Japanese attack and from the rescue work it interrupted. This is friendly fire, not a new encounter with a Japanese ship.

Patterson challenged an approaching radar contact, cast off from Canberra and illuminated it. Chicago gun crews fired toward the light and Patterson replied before emergency recognition ended the exchange.
The reports differ over the correctness of Patterson’s recognition signal. The directory does not decide that signaling dispute or convert the lack of reported hits into casualties.

title: American destroyers rescue Canberra’s crew and scuttle the cruiser
location: Southeast of Savo Island and the Guadalcanal transport area, Solomon Islands
summary: Patterson assisted firefighting aboard the disabled Australian cruiser Canberra, and Patterson and Blue evacuated its survivors. After evacuation, Selfridge and Ellet used gunfire and torpedoes to sink the abandoned cruiser.

sources.title: Office of Naval Intelligence — The Battle of Savo Island (1943), official NHHC 2017 republication, End of the Canberra, printed pp.29–31 / PDF pp.47–49
Royal Australian Navy — The Battle of Savo Island, evacuation and ordered scuttling of HMAS Canberra

U.S. Naval War College — The Battle of Savo Island, August 9th, 1942: Strategical and Tactical Analysis (1950), original scanned volume, Patterson firefighting, evacuation and Blue’s assistance, printed pp.288–289 / PDF pp.358–359

researchNotes: Dates follow the local operational calendar. These contacts occurred after midnight on August 9 within the night commonly called August 8–9; incompatible exact clock minutes in the reports are not treated as independent engagements.

An American rescue and scuttling operation for an Allied Australian ship, explicitly linked to its damage in the southern-group action. It does not count Canberra as an additional Japanese sinking during the earlier gun exchange.
Patterson passed hoses and pumping equipment and removed wounded; Blue helped complete evacuation. Survivors were transferred to the invasion transports. No single-ship rescue total is imposed.
Orders required destroying Canberra if it could not join the planned retirement. Selfridge’s initial gunfire and torpedoes did not immediately sink it; Ellet completed the ordered scuttling.
The Chicago–Patterson friendly-fire exchange interrupted this operation and has a separate contact record. Exact shell and torpedo-expenditure counts are omitted.

title: Rescue and salvage after Savo’s northern-force losses
location: Waters east and southeast of Savo Island, Solomon Islands
summary: American destroyers recovered survivors of Quincy, Vincennes and Astoria while Astoria’s crew and assisting ships attempted to save the damaged cruiser. Towing and firefighting failed to prevent Astoria’s sinking around midday, and the remaining salvage party was rescued.

sources.title: Office of Naval Intelligence — The Battle of Savo Island (1943), official NHHC 2017 republication, destroyer rescues and End of the Astoria, printed pp.29–33 / PDF pp.47–51

U.S. Naval War College — The Battle of Savo Island, August 9th, 1942: Strategical and Tactical Analysis (1950), original scanned volume, Astoria salvage and destroyer rescues, printed pp.291–296 / PDF pp.361–366

researchNotes: Dates follow the local operational calendar. These contacts occurred after midnight on August 9 within the night commonly called August 8–9; incompatible exact clock minutes in the reports are not treated as independent engagements.
A grouped rescue and salvage phase following the northern-force engagement, not a separate battle for each cruiser casualty or a successful recovery of Astoria.
Ellet, Bagley, Mugford, Helm and Wilson rescued men from the northern-force cruisers; their overlapping recoveries are not added into an unsupported unique-survivor total.

Astoria’s crew fought fires, evacuated wounded and returned a salvage party aboard. Hopkins actually took the cruiser in tow for a period, and Wilson supplied firefighting assistance. Source accounts differ over the exact towing and assistance times, so only the morning sequence is used.
Buchanan and Alchiba eventually recovered the remaining salvage party. Alchiba had been dispatched to tow, but this is not represented as a completed tow of Astoria.

Unidentified submarine contacts disrupted rescue work; they are not evidence of a confirmed Japanese submarine or a sinking. Astoria’s loss follows damage from the existing Savo action, not renewed Japanese gunfire around midday.

title: George F. Elliott firefighting, evacuation and attempted scuttling
location: Lunga Roads and the Guadalcanal transport area, Solomon Islands
summary: After an attacking aircraft crashed into George F. Elliott, Hull supplied firefighting water and tried unsuccessfully to tow the burning transport. Boats and Dewey helped remove the remaining personnel. Hull then attempted to sink the abandoned ship on Admiral Turner’s orders.

sources.title: Office of Naval Intelligence — The Landing in the Solomons, 7–8 August 1942 (1943; official NHHC 2017 republication), printed p. 70 (PDF p. 88), including the Betelgeuse war-diary footnote
Robert J. Cressman — Official Chronology of the U.S. Navy in World War II, 1942, August 7–9 entries

aliases: USS George F. Elliott (AP-13) salvage and evacuation
Hull and Dewey assistance to George F. Elliott
researchNotes: The August 8–9 interval describes rescue, firefighting and disposal attempts after the air attack. It is not a claim that the transport sank on a precisely verified day or that an air attack continued for two days.

The 1943 narrative says Hull could make no progress with a towline and continued pumping water. It reports that the torpedoes fired to scuttle Elliott had no effect and that the transport remained afloat and burning when the transports withdrew the following evening. The later Navy chronology says Elliott was eventually scuttled by Hull. These accounts do not independently establish an exact final sinking time here.

The Navy chronology groups Jarvis and Elliott as torpedoed; the detailed landing narrative establishes an aircraft crash and fire aboard Elliott without establishing an additional torpedo hit. No second damage mechanism is asserted.

The Betelgeuse war-diary extract describes its tank lighter TR-9 helping transfer wounded, survivors and records. This connected ship-rescue episode is distinct from the original air attack and from Marine amphibian-tractor work at Gavutu. Personnel and casualty totals are not adopted.

title: Bagley comes under fire from downed Japanese aircrew
summary: During aircrew-recovery activity after the August 8 raid, Bagley approached Japanese airmen on a partly submerged aircraft. The wartime Navy narrative reports that they fired on the destroyer; the encounter ended without their capture.

sources.title: Office of Naval Intelligence — The Landing in the Solomons, 7–8 August 1942 (1943; official NHHC 2017 republication), printed p. 71 (PDF p. 89), afternoon aircrew-recovery paragraph

aliases: USS Bagley (DD-386) encounter with downed Japanese airmen
researchNotes: This is an attributed report of gunfire directed at an American ship during the aftermath of the August 8 air raid, rather than an additional bombing attack or a claim that every rescue attempt involved fighting.

The narrative reports that the airmen then turned their guns on themselves. It does not establish their number, aircraft identity or unit, and no casualty tally or American return fire is asserted here.

The date follows the narrative’s afternoon-of-August-8 sequence. Other prisoner recoveries by Selfridge, Blue and an unnamed ship are contextual recovery operations, not extra hostile encounters within this record.

title: Hull fires on a motor schooner west of Kukum
location: West of Kukum, Guadalcanal, Solomon Islands
summary: The wartime Savo narrative reports that Hull used her main battery to sink a small motor schooner west of Kukum on August 9. The vessel was then suspected of directing Japanese troop movements, but its identity and hostile role were not established in that account.

sources.title: Office of Naval Intelligence — The Battle of Savo Island, 9 August 1942 (1943; official NHHC 2017 republication), printed p. 27 (PDF p. 45), Blue patrol and schooner paragraph

aliases: USS Hull (DD-350) motor-schooner contact off Kukum
researchNotes: The documented American firing is indexed with the source’s uncertainty about the target. This is not a confirmed named Japanese warship loss or a verified enemy troop-transport operation.

Blue earlier described a small two-masted motor schooner as harmless. The narrative only suggests it might have been the same vessel later fired on by Hull; that proposed identification is not treated as established.

The source dates Hull’s action to August 9 without a clock time. The earlier Blue sighting does not supply an exact time for Hull’s subsequent firing. No crew nationality or casualty count is assigned.

title: Henley depth-charges an unidentified sound contact
location: Approach to the Guadalcanal transport area after patrol off Tulagi, Solomon Islands
summary: While returning toward the Guadalcanal transport area around dawn after the Savo battle, Henley made a sound contact and dropped depth charges. The wartime narrative reports no positive result, and the target was not independently identified.

sources.title: Office of Naval Intelligence — The Battle of Savo Island, 9 August 1942 (1943; official NHHC 2017 republication), printed p. 28 (PDF p. 46), Our Destroyers, final paragraph

aliases: USS Henley (DD-391) unidentified antisubmarine contact, August 9, 1942
researchNotes: The recorded event is an American antisubmarine attack on a sound contact. It does not establish that an enemy submarine was present, damaged or sunk, and is therefore indexed as an operation rather than a confirmed submarine battle.

The narrative places the attack during Henley’s return toward the beach after a confused search for Australia, around dawn on August 9. Its earlier near-collision with Mugford is not treated as a separate combat encounter.

The ship’s own action report or deck log remains a follow-up for the contact’s exact time, position and classification. No submarine identity is inferred from the later presence of Japanese submarines elsewhere in the campaign.

title: Brush patrol action on the Koli Point–Tetere coastal track
location: Koli Point–Tetere coastal track, eastern Guadalcanal
summary: A patrol from Company A, 1st Marines, led by Captain Charles H. Brush attacked a Japanese advance party along the coast east of the Lunga perimeter. Frontal and flanking attacks defeated the party, and recovered maps and communications material warned the Marines that newly arrived Japanese forces were preparing an attack.

sources.title: John L. Zimmerman — The Guadalcanal Campaign (official Marine Corps monograph, 1949), Chapter IV, printed pp. 61–69
Hough, Ludwig and Shaw — Pearl Harbor to Guadalcanal (official Marine Corps history, 1958), Part VI, Chapter 4, printed pp. 283–291

researchNotes: The patrol followed reports passed through Father Arthur Duhamel, coastwatcher Martin Clemens and Solomon Islander scouts. Brush and Lieutenant John J. Jachym led the Marine action on August 19; the earlier survey and warning journeys were its background.

The 1949 account places the encounter between two unnamed villages on the coastal route toward Koli Point and Tetere; the revised 1958 history describes it as near Koli Point. Both describe fighting between the road and the beach.

Recovered documents and maps showed Japanese knowledge of Marine dispositions. The later history identifies Japanese Army insignia and ship-to-shore communications material as evidence that this was a newly arrived force.
This patrol action preceded the Japanese assault at Alligator Creek on the night of August 20–21. The simultaneous Matanikau and Kokumbona operations took place west of the Marine perimeter.

title: Relief patrol searches for Goettge’s party
location: Point Cruz–Matanikau coast and inland route to the Lunga perimeter, Guadalcanal, Solomon Islands
summary: Company A, 5th Marines, went by boat to search for Goettge’s missing patrol and was reinforced by elements of Company L and a machine-gun section. After landing west of Point Cruz, the force returned east by coastal and inland routes. The coastal party met Japanese resistance near the Matanikau, but neither group found the missing patrol.

sources.title: John L. Zimmerman — The Guadalcanal Campaign (official USMC monograph, 1949), Chapter IV, printed p. 60 (original PDF p. 73)
Hough, Ludwig and Shaw — Pearl Harbor to Guadalcanal (official USMC history, 1958), Part VI Chapter 4, printed p. 281 (original PDF p. 285)

aliases: Company A and Company L search west of the Matanikau, August 13–14, 1942
researchNotes: The search was sent out after the first survivor reported on the morning of August 13. The three known survivors returned independently; this operation is not represented as their rescue.

Company A returned by the coastal road on the evening of August 13 after minor resistance near the river mouth. Company L’s inland party, delayed by difficult terrain, reached the perimeter on August 14. The two-day interval includes movement rather than continuous fighting.

The separate routes and reinforcement belong to one connected relief/search operation. The original night ambush remains its parent, and the later August 19 offensive is a different planned operation.

The histories identify the Marine units and movement by boat, but do not establish the service affiliation of each boat crew here. No successful recovery, exact casualty total or additional Japanese defeat is inferred.

title: First Marine squadrons establish combat air operations at Henderson Field
summary: Nineteen F4F Wildcats of VMF-223 and twelve SBD dive bombers of VMSB-232 flew from Long Island to Henderson Field. The arrival of the first Marine combat squadrons gave the Guadalcanal beachhead a locally based fighter and dive-bomber force. Marine engineers and Navy CUB-1 personnel had prepared the field and ground services under difficult supply conditions.

August 20 and the 19-fighter/12-dive-bomber complement agree in the official Marine histories and Navy chronology. These are aircraft arriving, not enemy losses.
CUB-1 personnel had arrived on August 15 to prepare and service the aircraft. Navy participation also included the carrier ferry and launch.
Marine fighters supported the Tenaru ground battle on August 21. A separate aerial patrol encountered Japanese fighters north of Savo the same day.

title: VMF-223’s first aerial combat north of Savo Island
location: North of Savo Island and Henderson Field, Solomon Islands
summary: Around midday, four VMF-223 Wildcats patrolling from Henderson Field encountered six Japanese Zero fighters north of Savo Island. John L. Smith was credited with one Zero. Damaged Wildcats returned to Henderson, including aircraft that crash-landed. The encounter began the squadron’s air-to-air fighting from Guadalcanal, one day after its arrival.

researchNotes: The official aviation booklet places this patrol north of Savo, heading toward the Russell Islands, at about midday on August 21. This is geographically and operationally distinct from the same day’s beach strafing in support of the Tenaru battle.

The histories describe damaged and crash-landed Wildcats; temporary unserviceability did not necessarily mean a permanent aircraft loss.
The squadron history describes one lost F4F, while Mersky gives a more detailed account of several damaged aircraft. Exact repair and permanent-loss dispositions remain uncertain.

title: First Army Air Forces fighter detachment arrives at Henderson Field
summary: Five P-400 fighters of the 67th Fighter Squadron reached Henderson Field, bringing the first Army Air Forces aircraft to be based with the island’s Marine air units. The detachment expanded the force later known as the Cactus Air Force. The P-400s’ altitude and oxygen-equipment limitations restricted their usefulness against high-flying Japanese aircraft.

Official histories give different approximate operating ceilings for the P-400 under local oxygen limitations, while agreeing that these restrictions hampered high-altitude interception.
The squadron later undertook low-level reconnaissance and ground support. Its arrival on August 22 does not by itself establish a combat engagement that day.

title: Army B-17s attack destroyers off Guadalcanal and Tulagi
